future_direction: Building accurate and interpretable models to increase the range of model-based interpretability.
Developing tools for feature engineering to improve the usefulness of model-based interpretations.
Research on what form interpretations of black-box models should take and how to use post-hoc interpretations to improve predictive accuracy.
papers.abstract: Machine-learning models have demonstrated great success in learning complex patterns that enable them to make predictions about unobserved data. In addition to using models for prediction, the ability to interpret what a model has learned is receiving an increasing amount of attention. However, this increased focus has led to considerable confusion about the notion of interpretability. In particular, it is unclear how the wide array of proposed interpretation methods are related and what common concepts can be used to evaluate them. We aim to address these concerns by defining interpretability in the context of machine learning and introducing the predictive, descriptive, relevant (PDR) framework for discussing interpretations. The PDR framework provides 3 overarching desiderata for evaluation: predictive accuracy, descriptive accuracy, and relevancy, with relevancy judged relative to a human audience. Moreover, to help manage the deluge of interpretation methods, we introduce a categorization of existing techniques into model-based and post hoc categories, with subgroups including sparsity, modularity, and simulatability. To demonstrate how practitioners can use the PDR framework to evaluate and understand interpretations, we provide numerous real-world examples. These examples highlight the often underappreciated role played by human audiences in discussions of interpretability. Finally, based on our framework, we discuss limitations of existing methods and directions for future work. We hope that this work will provide a common vocabulary that will make it easier for both practitioners and researchers to discuss and choose from the full range of interpretation methods.

papers.title: Text-Trained LLMs Can Zero-Shot Extrapolate PDE Dynamics, Revealing a Three-Stage In-Context Learning Mechanism
papers.research_question: Can text-trained LLMs zero-shot extrapolate PDE dynamics, and what is the in-context learning mechanism behind this capability?
papers.core_contribution: Text-trained LLMs can zero-shot extrapolate PDE dynamics, and the in-context learning process follows a three-stage progression from syntax imitation to exploratory high-entropy phase to confident prediction.
papers.conclusion: Text-trained LLMs exhibit emergent zero-shot capability to extrapolate PDE dynamics, and the in-context learning process follows a consistent three-stage progression, revealing inductive biases analogous to numerical methods.
papers.key_findings:
One-step prediction accuracy improves with longer temporal context but degrades with finer spatial discretization.
Multi-step rollouts show algebraic error growth with time horizon, similar to classical numerical solvers.
Token-level entropy analysis reveals a three-stage ICL progression: syntax imitation, exploratory high-entropy phase, and confident prediction.
LLMs can sustain coherent multi-step rollouts for nonlinear PDEs like Allen-Cahn and wave equations.
The three-stage progression is consistent across model sizes and PDE types.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated emergent in-context learning (ICL) capabilities across a range of tasks, including zero-shot time-series forecasting. We show that text-trained foundation models can accurately extrapolate spatiotemporal dynamics from discretized partial differential equation (PDE) solutions without fine-tuning or natural language prompting. Predictive accuracy improves with longer temporal contexts but degrades at finer spatial discretizations. In multi-step rollouts, where the model recursively predicts future spatial states over multiple time steps, errors grow algebraically with the time horizon, reminiscent of global error accumulation in classical finite-difference solvers. We interpret these trends as in-context neural scaling laws, where prediction quality varies predictably with both context length and output length. To better understand how LLMs are able to internally process PDE solutions so as to accurately roll them out, we analyze token-level output distributions and uncover a consistent three-stage ICL progression: beginning with syntactic pattern imitation, transitioning through an exploratory high-entropy phase, and culminating in confident, numerically grounded predictions.

papers.title: The Next Five Hurdles What is a Linear Representation? What is a Multidimensional Feature? The Dark Matter of Neural Networks? Attention Pivot Tables Measuring feature sensitivity using dataset filtering
papers.research_question: What are the major hurdles facing mechanistic interpretability, and how can we improve feature analysis and measurement?
papers.core_contribution: This blog post outlines five key hurdles in mechanistic interpretability, refines the concept of linear representations to include multidimensional features, introduces the idea of 'dark matter' features, provides practical guidance for using attention pivot tables, and demonstrates a method to measure feature sensitivity using LLM-assisted dataset filtering.
papers.conclusion: The authors are optimistic about progress in mechanistic interpretability despite challenges, and highlight the need for further research into feature cooperation and improved analysis methods.
papers.key_findings:
Current sparse autoencoder methods may miss many rare features, suggesting a 'dark matter' of neural networks that is difficult to observe.
Linear representations can be mathematically linear even with multidimensional features, requiring a revised definition.
Attention pivot tables reveal interpretable skip-trigrams in one-layer transformers, but their clarity depends on training details and dataset.
Feature sensitivity measured via Claude-filtered datasets shows that individual features often have low sensitivity, and concepts are represented by multiple cooperating features.
Different versions of Claude agree well with each other and with human judgments when rating concept relevance in text snippets.
papers.limitation:
Dictionary learning may be unable to resolve extremely rare features, limiting comprehensiveness.
Features identified by sparse autoencoders often have imperfect sensitivity and specificity, with concepts distributed across multiple features.
Attention pivot table results are sensitive to training hyperparameters and dataset composition, making interpretation unreliable under suboptimal conditions.
future_direction: Developing more efficient dictionary learning algorithms to capture rare features.
Automating the discovery of complementary features that collectively represent concepts.
Further investigation into attention superposition and cross-layer superposition.
papers.abstract: What are the major hurdles facing mechanistic interpretability, and how can we improve feature analysis and measurement? This blog post outlines five key hurdles in mechanistic interpretability, refines the concept of linear representations to include multidimensional features, introduces the idea of 'dark matter' features, provides practical guidance for using attention pivot tables, and demonstrates a method to measure feature sensitivity using LLM-assisted dataset filtering. The authors are optimistic about progress in mechanistic interpretability despite challenges, and highlight the need for further research into feature cooperation and improved analysis methods.

papers.title: BERTology Meets Biology: Interpreting Attention in Protein Language Models
papers.research_question: What does attention in protein Transformer language models capture about protein structure and function?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that attention in protein language models captures high-level structural and functional properties of proteins, and that attention focuses on progressively more complex properties with increasing layer depth.
papers.conclusion: Attention in protein Transformer models recovers structural and functional properties of proteins, and interpretability methods can aid scientific discovery.
papers.key_findings:
Attention in deep layers aligns with contact maps, connecting amino acids that are spatially close in 3D structure but far in sequence.
Attention targets binding sites and post-translational modifications, key functional components.
Attention heads specialize in particular amino acids and their patterns are consistent with substitution matrices.
Deeper layers focus more on high-level properties (binding sites, contacts) while secondary structure is targeted more evenly across layers.
Knowledge in embeddings accumulates gradually over layers, while attention acquires knowledge primarily in final layers.
papers.limitation: The analyses are associative and do not establish causal links between attention and model behavior.
future_direction: Using attention and learned representations as tools for scientific discovery.
Developing contextual visualizations of learned representations for domain experts in scientific domains.
papers.abstract: Abstract Transformer architectures have proven to learn useful representations for protein classification and generation tasks. However, these representations present challenges in interpretability. Through the lens of attention, we analyze the inner workings of the Transformer and explore how the model discerns structural and functional properties of proteins. We show that attention (1) captures the folding structure of proteins, connecting amino acids that are far apart in the underlying sequence, but spatially close in the three-dimensional structure, (2) targets binding sites, a key functional component of proteins, and (3) focuses on progressively more complex biophysical properties with increasing layer depth. We also present a three-dimensional visualization of the interaction between attention and protein structure. Our findings align with known biological processes and provide a tool to aid discovery in protein engineering and synthetic biology. The code for visualization and analysis is available at https://github.com/salesforce/provis .

papers.title: A Categorisation of Post-hoc Explanations for Predictive Models
papers.research_question: How can post-hoc explanations for predictive models be categorized to aid model interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: Extends and tests a hierarchical categorization of post-hoc explanation techniques for interpretability of predictive models.
papers.conclusion: The article provides an overview of interpretability aspects, proposes a categorization, and highlights areas for future research such as bug-free models and axiomatic treatments.
papers.key_findings:
Proposes a hierarchical view of interpretability with transparency and post-hoc explanations as main categories.
Identifies a lack of clear distinction between interpretability and debugability in existing literature.
Categorizes post-hoc explanations into Group A (what the model learned) and Group B (why specific predictions are made), each with model-agnostic and model-specific subgroups.
papers.limitation: Lack of clear distinction between interpretability and debugability in existing methodologies.
future_direction: Constructing bug-free predictive models to potentially alleviate the need for interpretability.
Work towards an axiomatic treatment of interpretability.
papers.abstract: The ubiquity of machine learning based predictive models in modern society naturally leads people to ask how trustworthy those models are? In predictive modeling, it is quite common to induce a trade-off between accuracy and interpretability. For instance, doctors would like to know how effective some treatment will be for a patient or why the model suggested a particular medication for a patient exhibiting those symptoms? We acknowledge that the necessity for interpretability is a consequence of an incomplete formalisation of the problem, or more precisely of multiple meanings adhered to a particular concept. For certain problems, it is not enough to get the answer (what), the model also has to provide an explanation of how it came to that conclusion (why), because a correct prediction, only partially solves the original problem. In this article we extend existing categorisation of techniques to aid model interpretability and test this categorisation.

papers.title: Layer-wise Relevance Propagation for Echo State Networks applied to Earth System Variability
papers.research_question: How can Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) be applied to Echo State Networks (ESNs) to make them interpretable, and how does this apply to the detection of El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO) from sea surface temperature anomalies?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates how Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) can be applied to Echo State Networks (ESNs) to interpret their decisions, and shows that the leak rate in the reservoir is a crucial parameter controlling memory and performance.
papers.conclusion: LRP can be applied to ESNs to open the black-box, and ESNs are effective for image classification tasks like ENSO detection, with advantages in training speed and parameter efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
LRP can be successfully applied to ESNs, providing relevance maps that highlight important input regions for classification.
The leak rate in the reservoir determines the memory time scale; too high leak rate causes the model to forget early inputs and performance drops.
ESNs achieve competitive accuracy with fewer trainable parameters compared to MLP, reducing overfitting risks.
The model focuses on the Niño 3.4 region for ENSO detection, which is physically reasonable.
The model is robust to random permutation of input columns, indicating it does not rely on the zonal structure of the data.
future_direction: Apply further xAI techniques (backward optimization, sensitivity analysis, salience maps) to ESN models.
Use ESN models for time series prediction with LRP as an alternative to attention mechanisms.
Apply ESNs with LRP to unsolved problems in climate and ocean science.
papers.abstract: Artificial neural networks (ANNs) are known to be powerful methods for many hard problems (e.g. image classification, speech recognition or time series prediction). However, these models tend to produce black-box results and are often difficult to interpret. Layer-wise relevance propagation (LRP) is a widely used technique to understand how ANN models come to their conclusion and to understand what a model has learned. Here, we focus on Echo State Networks (ESNs) as a certain type of recurrent neural networks, also known as reservoir computing. ESNs are easy to train and only require a small number of trainable parameters, but are still black-box models. We show how LRP can be applied to ESNs in order to open the black-box. We also show how ESNs can be used not only for time series prediction but also for image classification: Our ESN model serves as a detector for El Nino Southern Oscillation (ENSO) from sea surface temperature anomalies. ENSO is actually a well-known problem and has been extensively discussed before. But here we use this simple problem to demonstrate how LRP can significantly enhance the explainablility of ESNs.

papers.title: Towards Open-Ended Visual Scientific Discovery with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can enable open-ended feature discovery from foundation model representations.
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders can systematically recover semantic structure from foundation model representations without concept supervision, enabling open-ended feature discovery for scientific exploration.
papers.conclusion: SAEs provide a practical method for extracting interpretable features from vision foundation models, supporting open-ended discovery in scientific domains where target concepts are not pre-specified.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs outperform k-means and PCA on concept alignment metrics like mAP, Purity@k, and Coverage@τ.
Matryoshka SAEs achieve higher class coverage than standard SAEs on ADE20K.
SAEs can recover fine-grained anatomical parts from ecological images without labels.
Larger foundation models and later transformer layers lead to better concept rediscovery despite being harder to reconstruct.
Concept prevalence affects rediscovery; more common parts are recovered more reliably.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation relies on ground-truth annotations to measure concept alignment, limiting assessment in truly unannotated domains.
Only visual examples are used to describe features; future work might use multimodal LLMs for language descriptions.
future_direction: Systematic evaluation of novel discoveries in unannotated domains.
Applying SAEs to non-vision foundation models.
papers.abstract: Scientific archives now contain hundreds of petabytes of data across genomics, ecology, climate, and molecular biology that could reveal undiscovered patterns if systematically analyzed at scale. Large-scale, weakly-supervised datasets in language and vision have driven the development of foundation models whose internal representations encode structure (patterns, co-occurrences and statistical regularities) beyond their training objectives. Most existing methods extract structure only for pre-specified targets; they excel at confirmation but do not support open-ended discovery of unknown patterns. We ask whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can enable open-ended feature discovery from foundation model representations. We evaluate this question in controlled rediscovery studies, where the learned SAE features are tested for alignment with semantic concepts on a standard segmentation benchmark and compared against strong label-free alternatives on concept-alignment metrics. Applied to ecological imagery, the same procedure surfaces fine-grained anatomical structure without access to segmentation or part labels, providing a scientific case study with ground-truth validation. While our experiments focus on vision with an ecology case study, the method is domain-agnostic and applicable to models in other sciences (e.g., proteins, genomics, weather). Our results indicate that sparse decomposition provides a practical instrument for exploring what scientific foundation models have learned, an important prerequisite for moving from confirmation to genuine discovery.

papers.title: Generalization vs. Memorization in Autoregressive Deep Learning: Or, Examining Temporal Decay of Gradient Coherence
papers.research_question: How can we distinguish between genuine generalization and mere memorization in autoregressive PDE emulators? What are the limitations of standard models and training routines in achieving generalization?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces influence-based diagnostics to show that autoregressive PDE emulators fail to learn a globally consistent solution operator, instead memorizing time- and class-specific patterns, and provides insights for improving generalization.
papers.conclusion: Current physics-agnostic PDE emulators fail to internalize the governing equations, and influence functions provide a diagnostic framework to distinguish memorization from generalization, highlighting the need for physics-based constraints or architectural changes.
papers.key_findings:
Autoregressive PDE emulators exhibit rapid decay of off-diagonal influence, indicating gradient responses are localized in time and class.
Both UNet and ViT models fail to support nontrivial off-diagonal response, meaning they do not learn a shared feature basis across trajectories.
Gradient geometry is class-locked, with limited inter-class influence, showing that models treat different initial conditions as separate tasks.
The neural tangent kernel spectrum reveals a stiff, anisotropic geometry, indicating that low test error coexists with sharp, high-curvature directions rather than robust generalization.
The models behave as statistical estimators that interpolate within neighborhoods of the training data, rather than learning the underlying physical laws.
future_direction: Incorporate physics-based constraints as regularizers or architectural biases to improve generalization.
papers.abstract: Foundation models trained as autoregressive PDE surrogates hold significant promise for accelerating scientific discovery through their capacity to both extrapolate beyond training regimes and efficiently adapt to downstream tasks despite a paucity of examples for fine-tuning. However, reliably achieving genuine generalization - a necessary capability for producing novel scientific insights and robustly performing during deployment - remains a critical challenge. Establishing whether or not these requirements are met demands evaluation metrics capable of clearly distinguishing genuine model generalization from mere memorization. We apply the influence function formalism to systematically characterize how autoregressive PDE surrogates assimilate and propagate information derived from diverse physical scenarios, revealing fundamental limitations of standard models and training routines in addition to providing actionable insights regarding the design of improved surrogates.

papers.title: Self-Supervised Vision Transformers Learn Visual Concepts in Histopathology
papers.research_question: Can self-supervised learning, particularly DINO-based knowledge distillation, learn data-efficient and interpretable features in histology images?
papers.core_contribution: Vision Transformers using DINO-based self-supervised learning learn data-efficient and interpretable features in histology images, with different attention heads capturing distinct morphological phenotypes.
papers.conclusion: Self-supervised learning, particularly DINO, is effective for learning representations in histopathology, and the attention heads of Vision Transformers provide interpretable visual concepts that can aid in biomarker discovery.
papers.key_findings:
ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-50 features are a strong baseline, achieving comparable performance to self-supervised methods on many tasks.
Self-supervised features, particularly from DINO, are robust and sample-efficient, performing well with less training data.
DINO outperforms SimCLR on weakly-supervised and patch-level tasks in histopathology.
DINO's attention heads learn distinct morphological visual concepts, localizing cells, stroma tissue, and fat/air pockets.
papers.limitation: Performance benefit of self-supervised learning may vary depending on organ type (only breast tissue tested) and weakly-supervised architecture (only CLAM tested).
future_direction: Assess the utility of self-supervised methods for learning representations of histopathological images from rare diseases with data paucity of slide-level and patch-level annotations.
papers.abstract: Tissue phenotyping is a fundamental task in learning objective characterizations of histopathologic biomarkers within the tumor-immune microenvironment in cancer pathology. However, whole-slide imaging (WSI) is a complex computer vision in which: 1) WSIs have enormous image resolutions with precludes large-scale pixel-level efforts in data curation, and 2) diversity of morphological phenotypes results in inter- and intra-observer variability in tissue labeling. To address these limitations, current efforts have proposed using pretrained image encoders (transfer learning from ImageNet, self-supervised pretraining) in extracting morphological features from pathology, but have not been extensively validated. In this work, we conduct a search for good representations in pathology by training a variety of self-supervised models with validation on a variety of weakly-supervised and patch-level tasks. Our key finding is in discovering that Vision Transformers using DINO-based knowledge distillation are able to learn data-efficient and interpretable features in histology images wherein the different attention heads learn distinct morphological phenotypes. We make evaluation code and pretrained weights publicly-available at: https://github.com/Richarizardd/Self-Supervised-ViT-Path.

papers.title: Using data assimilation tools to dissect GraphDOP
papers.research_question: How can Data Assimilation (DA) diagnostic tools, such as Forecast Sensitivity-based Observation Impact (FSOI), be applied to Machine Learning models to enhance their interpretability and explainability?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that Data Assimilation diagnostic tools (FSOI and sensitivity analysis) can be successfully transferred to ML models like GraphDOP, enhancing interpretability and explainability by showing the model captures physically meaningful processes.
papers.conclusion: Data Assimilation diagnostic tools, particularly FSOI, are effective for interpreting and explaining the GraphDOP model, confirming it captures real physical processes and constructs a coherent internal representation from heterogeneous observational data.
papers.key_findings:
GraphDOP's sliding attention window learns meteorological features and spatial relationships from observation data.
GraphDOP uses information from satellite radiances (e.g., ATMS channels) to predict surface variables like 2-meter temperature.
GraphDOP tracks the movement of storm systems (e.g., extratropical storms) by shifting its attention with forecast lead time, similar to physical dynamics.
FSOI analysis reveals GraphDOP builds a coherent internal representation of the Earth system by blending information from conventional and satellite observations.
Some satellite channels (e.g., ATMS channel 22) have a larger impact on reducing forecast error, while others (e.g., channels 4 and 17) can increase error.
papers.limitation: The results are based on a version of GraphDOP trained on a limited selection of observation types to reduce computational cost, not the full state-of-the-art model.
future_direction: Replicate the study with the current state-of-the-art GraphDOP model to evaluate the importance of different observation types.
Use the presented tools to benchmark the quality of different AI-DOP models, ensuring they provide correct forecasts for the right reasons.
Implement an online observation Quality Control (QC) mechanism based on the impact measured by the FSOI diagnostic.
papers.abstract: The Data Assimilation (DA) community has been developing various diagnostics to understand the importance of the observing system in accurately forecasting the weather. They usually rely on the ability to compute the derivatives of the physical model output with respect to its initial condition. For example, the Forecast Sensitivity-based Observation Impact (FSOI) estimates the impact on the forecast error of each observation processed in the DA system. This paper presents how these DA diagnostic tools are transferred to Machine Learning (ML) models, as their derivatives are readily available through automatic differentiation. We specifically explore the interpretability and explainability of the observation-driven GraphDOP model developed at the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF). The interpretability study demonstrates the effectiveness of GraphDOP's sliding attention window to learn the meteorological features present in the observation datasets and to learn the spatial relationships between different regions. Making these relationships more transparent confirms that GraphDOP captures real, physically meaningful processes, such as the movement of storm systems. The explainability of GraphDOP is explored by applying the FSOI tool to study the impact of the different observations on the forecast error. This inspection reveals that GraphDOP creates an internal representation of the Earth system by combining the information from conventional and satellite observations.

papers.title: Systematic Evaluation of Single-Cell Foundation Model Interpretability Reveals Attention Captures Co-Expression Rather Than Unique Regulatory Signal
papers.research_question: Does attention in single-cell foundation models capture causal regulatory relationships or just co-expression? Do attention-derived edge scores provide incremental value beyond gene-level features for predicting perturbation outcomes?
papers.core_contribution: Attention patterns in single-cell foundation models encode structured biological information (e.g., protein-protein interactions in early layers, transcriptional regulation in late layers) but do not capture causal regulatory signal; they provide no incremental value over gene-level features for predicting perturbation outcomes.
papers.conclusion: Attention patterns in single-cell foundation models capture co-expression rather than causal regulatory signal, and the proposed evaluation framework provides a reusable quality-control standard for mechanistic interpretability in this domain.
papers.key_findings:
Attention patterns show layer-specific biological specialization but do not outperform trivial gene-level baselines for perturbation prediction.
Pairwise edge scores (attention or correlation) provide no incremental predictive value beyond gene-level features.
Causal ablation of 'regulatory' attention heads does not degrade perturbation prediction, indicating distributed redundancy.
The relationship between attention and correlation is context-dependent across cell types and perturbation modalities.
Cell-State Stratified Interpretability (CSSI) improves attention-derived GRN recovery by controlling for heterogeneity.
papers.limitation:
Causal ablation only performed on Geneformer V2-316M, not on scGPT due to architectural differences.
Perturbation data limited to four cell types and two modalities; additional tissues, species, and architectures remain untested.
No decisive positive control demonstrates recovery of known causal regulatory structure in a realistic perturbation setting.
future_direction: Test additional tissues, species, and architectures (e.g., scFoundation).
Focus interpretability efforts on residual-stream geometry, MLP-stored knowledge, or representations from the full forward pass.
papers.abstract: We present a systematic evaluation framework - thirty-seven analyses, 153 statistical tests, four cell types, two perturbation modalities - for assessing mechanistic interpretability in single-cell foundation models. Applying this framework to scGPT and Geneformer, we find that attention patterns encode structured biological information with layer-specific organisation - protein-protein interactions in early layers, transcriptional regulation in late layers - but this structure provides no incremental value for perturbation prediction: trivial gene-level baselines outperform both attention and correlation edges (AUROC 0.81-0.88 versus 0.70), pairwise edge scores add zero predictive contribution, and causal ablation of regulatory heads produces no degradation. These findings generalise from K562 to RPE1 cells; the attention-correlation relationship is context-dependent, but gene-level dominance is universal. Cell-State Stratified Interpretability (CSSI) addresses an attention-specific scaling failure, improving GRN recovery up to 1.85x. The framework establishes reusable quality-control standards for the field.

papers.title: Trade-Offs in Fine-Tuned Diffusion Models between Accuracy and Interpretability
papers.research_question: Does fine-tuning diffusion models with a learnable text encoder affect their interpretability, and what is the trade-off between image fidelity and interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: Fine-tuning diffusion models with a learnable text encoder improves image quality but destroys interpretability (localization ability), while freezing the text encoder retains interpretability at a slight cost to image quality, revealing a trade-off.
papers.conclusion: The standard practice of fine-tuning diffusion models with a learnable text encoder leads to a loss of interpretability; freezing the text encoder preserves interpretability while maintaining reasonable generative performance, highlighting an important design consideration.
papers.key_findings:
Fine-tuning diffusion models with a learnable text encoder (Finetune L) yields high image quality (low FID) but poor interpretability (low localization metrics).
Fine-tuning with a frozen text encoder (Finetune F) retains strong interpretability (good localization) but results in slightly worse image quality.
The variability of text prompts impacts interpretability; higher variability (full impressions) leads to better interpretability than low variability (class labels).
The end-of-string (EOS) token often shows high localization performance, but only the frozen model learns to associate disease-describing tokens with correct image regions.
The trade-off between image fidelity and interpretability is demonstrated, suggesting interpretability should be considered when designing generative models for critical domains like medical imaging.
papers.limitation: FID has its own limitation due to it being a trained metric and requiring too many samples to be accurate, and conditional generation evaluation is limited as there is no ground-truth data available.
future_direction: Perform a large-scale study that analyses the quality of images judged by domain experts in relation to FID and CNR to see which metric better captures generative quality.
papers.abstract: Recent advancements in diffusion models have significantly impacted the trajectory of generative machine learning re-search, with many adopting the strategy of fine-tuning pre-trained models using domain-specific text-to-image datasets. Notably, this method has been readily employed for medical applications, such as X-ray image synthesis, leveraging the plethora of associated radiology reports. Yet, a prevailing concern is the lack of assurance on whether these models genuinely comprehend their generated content. With the evolution of text conditional image generation, these models have grown potent enough to facilitate object localization scrutiny. Our research underscores this advancement in the critical realm of medical imaging, emphasizing the crucial role of interpretability. We further unravel a consequential trade-off between image fidelity – as gauged by conventional metrics – and model interpretability in generative diffusion models. Specifically, the adoption of learnable text encoders when fine-tuning results in diminished interpretability. Our in-depth exploration uncovers the underlying factors responsible for this divergence. Consequently, we present a set of design principles for the development of truly interpretable generative models. Code is available at https://github.com/MischaD/chest-distillation.

papers.title: The Dead Salmons of AI Interpretability
papers.research_question: What are the failure modes and statistical fragilities of contemporary AI interpretability methods, and how can they be addressed through a statistical-causal reframing?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues for a statistical-causal reframing of AI interpretability, where explanations are treated as parameters of a statistical model inferred from computational traces, to address false discoveries and statistical fragility.
papers.conclusion: Situating interpretability within the standard toolkit of statistical inference opens promising avenues for turning AI interpretability into a pragmatic and rigorous science.
papers.key_findings:
Many interpretability methods (feature attribution, probing, sparse autoencoders, circuit discovery) produce plausible-looking explanations even when applied to randomly initialized neural networks, demonstrating 'dead salmon' artifacts.
Interpretability methods suffer from broader statistical fragility, including poor generalization, high variance, and sensitivity to experimental design choices.
The root cause of these issues is the non-identifiability of many interpretability queries, meaning computational traces do not uniquely determine explanations.
Hypothesis testing against randomized null models (e.g., comparing a trained network to a randomly initialized one) can mitigate dead salmon artifacts, as shown in probing experiments.
A formal statistical-causal framework, where explanations are surrogate models answering distributions of causal queries, provides a principled foundation for evaluating and improving interpretability methods.
future_direction: Active selection of queries to reduce uncertainty
Meta-analysis of interpretability studies
Bayesian uncertainty quantification for explanations
papers.abstract: In a striking neuroscience study, the authors placed a dead salmon in an MRI scanner and showed it images of humans in social situations. Astonishingly, standard analyses of the time reported brain regions predictive of social emotions. The explanation, of course, was not supernatural cognition but a cautionary tale about misapplied statistical inference. In AI interpretability, reports of similar ''dead salmon'' artifacts abound: feature attribution, probing, sparse auto-encoding, and even causal analyses can produce plausible-looking explanations for randomly initialized neural networks. In this work, we examine this phenomenon and argue for a pragmatic statistical-causal reframing: explanations of computational systems should be treated as parameters of a (statistical) model, inferred from computational traces. This perspective goes beyond simply measuring statistical variability of explanations due to finite sampling of input data; interpretability methods become statistical estimators, and findings should be tested against explicit and meaningful alternative computational hypotheses, with uncertainty quantified with respect to the postulated statistical model. It also highlights important theoretical issues, such as the identifiability of common interpretability queries, which we argue is critical to understand the field's susceptibility to false discoveries, poor generalizability, and high variance. More broadly, situating interpretability within the standard toolkit of statistical inference opens promising avenues for future work aimed at turning AI interpretability into a pragmatic and rigorous science.

papers.title: Interpretation of Prediction Models Using the Input Gradient
papers.research_question: How can we interpret the behavior of any predictive model? The paper proposes using the partial derivatives of the model with respect to the input to determine which variables affect the prediction and how.
papers.core_contribution: Proposes using the gradient of the model with respect to input features as a general method to interpret which input variables affect the prediction and how.
papers.conclusion: The gradient vector with respect to input is a useful quantity for interpreting model behavior, providing insights into feature importance and revealing global structure such as linearity.
papers.key_findings:
The gradient norm with respect to word embeddings in a CNN model can identify the most influential words or expressions for sentiment classification.
For a Bag-of-Words neural network, the average gradient over the test set provides a global ranking of word importance, revealing words like 'excellent' and 'worst' as most influential.
The average gradient vector can approximate the prediction function with 99.6% accuracy, indicating the decision boundary is nearly linear.
The gradient-based interpretation method is general and can be applied to any predictive model, including non-differentiable cases via numerical approximation.
The method is computationally efficient as gradients can be obtained via backpropagation.
papers.abstract: State of the art machine learning algorithms are highly optimized to provide the optimal prediction possible, naturally resulting in complex models. While these models often outperform simpler more interpretable models by order of magnitudes, in terms of understanding the way the model functions, we are often facing a "black box". In this paper we suggest a simple method to interpret the behavior of any predictive model, both for regression and classification. Given a particular model, the information required to interpret it can be obtained by studying the partial derivatives of the model with respect to the input. We exemplify this insight by interpreting convolutional and multi-layer neural networks in the field of natural language processing.

papers.title: BERTology Meets Biology: Interpreting Attention in Protein Language\n Models
papers.research_question: How does attention in protein Transformer models capture structural and functional properties of proteins?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that attention in protein Transformer models captures the folding structure of proteins, targets binding sites, and focuses on progressively more complex biophysical properties with increasing layer depth.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that attention in protein Transformer models recovers structural and functional properties of proteins, and that such interpretability methods can potentially aid scientific discovery in biology.
papers.key_findings:
Attention in protein Transformers captures tertiary structure (contact maps).
Attention targets functional sites like binding sites and post-translational modifications.
Deeper layers focus on more complex properties (e.g., binding sites, contacts) while secondary structure is targeted more evenly across layers.
Attention heads specialize in particular amino acids and their attention patterns correlate with substitution matrices.
The findings are consistent across multiple Transformer architectures (BERT, ALBERT, XLNet) and datasets.
papers.limitation: The analyses are associative and do not establish causal links between attention and model behavior.
future_direction: Leveraging attention to uncover novel relationships or more nuanced forms of existing measures such as contact maps.
Developing contextual visualizations of learned representations in other scientific domains.
papers.abstract:
Transformer architectures have proven to learn useful representations for
protein classification and generation tasks. However, these representations
present challenges in interpretability. In this work, we demonstrate a set of
methods for analyzing protein Transformer models through the lens of attention.
We show that attention: (1) captures the folding structure of proteins,
connecting amino acids that are far apart in the underlying sequence, but
spatially close in the three-dimensional structure, (2) targets binding sites,
a key functional component of proteins, and (3) focuses on progressively more
complex biophysical properties with increasing layer depth. We find this
behavior to be consistent across three Transformer architectures (BERT, ALBERT,
XLNet) and two distinct protein datasets. We also present a three-dimensional
visualization of the interaction between attention and protein structure. Code
for visualization and analysis is available at
https://github.com/salesforce/provis.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence in environmental and Earth system sciences: explainability and trustworthiness
papers.research_question: What is the current state of XAI applications in environmental and Earth system sciences, and how does XAI contribute to trust in AI?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a comprehensive review of 575 articles on explainable AI (XAI) applications in environmental and Earth system sciences, highlighting a critical gap between the use of XAI methods and the scientific investigation of trust in AI.
papers.conclusion: The review underlines the need for more studies on how to strengthen trust in AI applications and recommends developing a 'human-centered' XAI framework that incorporates the views and needs of multiple stakeholder groups for trustworthy decision-making.
papers.key_findings:
XAI applications are popular in various environmental domains including ecology, engineering, geology, remote sensing, and water resources.
SHAP and Shapley methods are the most popular XAI methods (135 articles), followed by feature importance, partial dependence plots, and LIME.
Only 1.2% of the reviewed studies (7 articles) addressed trustworthiness as a core research objective.
There is a critical knowledge gap in understanding the relationship between explainability and trust in AI for environmental decision-making.
While XAI applications continue to grow, they do not necessarily enhance trust, and more studies on strengthening trust are needed.
future_direction: More studies on how to strengthen trust in AI applications.
Developing human-centered XAI frameworks for trustworthy decision-making.
Adapting XAI methods for spatial and temporal data in environmental sciences.
papers.abstract: Abstract Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) methods have recently emerged to gain insights into complex machine learning models. XAI can be promising for environmental and Earth system science because high-stakes decision-making for management and planning requires justification based on evidence and systems understanding. However, an overview of XAI applications and trust in AI in environmental and Earth system science is still missing. To close this gap, we reviewed 575 articles. XAI applications are popular in various domains, including ecology, engineering, geology, remote sensing, water resources, meteorology, atmospheric sciences, geochemistry, and geophysics. XAI applications focused primarily on understanding and predicting anthropogenic changes in geospatial patterns and impacts on human society and natural resources, especially biological species distributions, vegetation, air quality, transportation, and climate-water related topics, including risk and management. Among XAI methods, the SHAP and Shapley methods were the most popular (135 articles), followed by feature importance (27), partial dependence plots (22), LIME (21), and saliency maps (15). Although XAI methods are often argued to increase trust in model predictions, only seven studies (1.2%) addressed trustworthiness as a core research objective. This gap is critical because understanding the relationship between explainability and trust is lacking. While XAI applications continue to grow, they do not necessarily enhance trust. Hence, more studies on how to strengthen trust in AI applications are critically needed. Finally, this review underlines the recommendation of developing a “human-centered” XAI framework that incorporates the distinct views and needs of multiple stakeholder groups to enable trustworthy decision-making.

papers.title: Resurrecting the Salmon: Rethinking Mechanistic Interpretability with Domain-Specific Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Does training sparse autoencoders on a narrow domain (medical text) improve reconstruction fidelity and interpretability compared to broad-domain SAEs?
papers.core_contribution: Training sparse autoencoders on a narrow domain (medical text) improves reconstruction fidelity, interpretability, and reduces linear residual error compared to broad-domain SAEs.
papers.conclusion: Domain-confinement mitigates key limitations of broad-domain SAEs, enabling more complete and interpretable latent decompositions, and suggests the field may need to question 'foundation-model' scaling for general-purpose SAEs.
papers.key_findings:
Domain-specific SAEs achieve 15-20% higher fraction of variance explained and better loss recovery than broad-domain SAEs.
Domain-specific SAEs produce features that are more interpretable and aligned with clinically meaningful concepts.
Domain-specific SAEs capture more linear structure, leaving a smaller and more nonlinear residual error (less dark matter).
Domain-specific SAEs show improved cosine similarity between activations and reconstructions.
Domain-specific SAEs have minimal shrinkage (relative reconstruction bias close to 1).
future_direction: Extending domain-specific SAEs to other specialised domains, such as legal or financial text.
Investigating how domain confinement affects feature splitting and absorption.
Studying the trade-offs between domain breadth and SAE performance.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose large language model (LLM) activations into latent features that reveal mechanistic structure. Conventional SAEs train on broad data distributions, forcing a fixed latent budget to capture only high-frequency, generic patterns. This often results in significant linear ``dark matter'' in reconstruction error and produces latents that fragment or absorb each other, complicating interpretation. We show that restricting SAE training to a well-defined domain (medical text) reallocates capacity to domain-specific features, improving both reconstruction fidelity and interpretability. Training JumpReLU SAEs on layer-20 activations of Gemma-2 models using 195k clinical QA examples, we find that domain-confined SAEs explain up to 20\% more variance, achieve higher loss recovery, and reduce linear residual error compared to broad-domain SAEs. Automated and human evaluations confirm that learned features align with clinically meaningful concepts (e.g., ``taste sensations'' or ``infectious mononucleosis''), rather than frequent but uninformative tokens. These domain-specific SAEs capture relevant linear structure, leaving a smaller, more purely nonlinear residual. We conclude that domain-confinement mitigates key limitations of broad-domain SAEs, enabling more complete and interpretable latent decompositions, and suggesting the field may need to question ``foundation-model'' scaling for general-purpose SAEs.

papers.title: Towards Unifying Interpretability and Control: Evaluation via Intervention
papers.research_question: How well can interpretability methods control model behavior through interventions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a unifying framework and two evaluation metrics (intervention success rate and coherence-intervention tradeoff) to assess interpretability methods' ability to control model behavior, finding that current methods are inconsistent and often compromise coherence.
papers.conclusion: Current interpretability methods have limitations in achieving control without degrading output quality, and lens-based methods are more effective for simple interventions.
papers.key_findings:
While current interpretability methods allow for intervention, their effectiveness is inconsistent across features and models.
Lens-based methods (Logit Lens and Tuned Lens) outperform SAEs and probes in achieving simple, concrete interventions.
Mechanistic interventions often compromise model coherence, underperforming simpler alternatives like prompting.
Sparse autoencoders have high error rates in feature labeling, leading to lower intervention success.
Probes and steering vectors learn spurious correlations, affecting their intervention performance.
papers.limitation: Interventions often compromise model coherence, leading to repetitive or incoherent outputs.
papers.abstract: With the growing complexity and capability of large language models, a need to understand model reasoning has emerged, often motivated by an underlying goal of controlling and aligning models. While numerous interpretability and steering methods have been proposed as solutions, they are typically designed either for understanding or for control, seldom addressing both. Additionally, the lack of standardized applications, motivations, and evaluation metrics makes it difficult to assess methods' practical utility and efficacy. To address the aforementioned issues, we argue that intervention is a fundamental goal of interpretability and introduce success criteria to evaluate how well methods can control model behavior through interventions. To evaluate existing methods for this ability, we unify and extend four popular interpretability methods-sparse autoencoders, logit lens, tuned lens, and probing-into an abstract encoder-decoder framework, enabling interventions on interpretable features that can be mapped back to latent representations to control model outputs. We introduce two new evaluation metrics: intervention success rate and coherence-intervention tradeoff, designed to measure the accuracy of explanations and their utility in controlling model behavior. Our findings reveal that (1) while current methods allow for intervention, their effectiveness is inconsistent across features and models, (2) lens-based methods outperform SAEs and probes in achieving simple, concrete interventions, and (3) mechanistic interventions often compromise model coherence, underperforming simpler alternatives, such as prompting, and highlighting a critical shortcoming of current interpretability approaches in applications requiring control.

papers.title: Open Problems in Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: What are the key open problems in mechanistic interpretability methods, applications, and socio-technical challenges that need to be addressed to achieve the field's goals?
papers.core_contribution: This review synthesizes and outlines key open problems in mechanistic interpretability, covering methods, applications, and socio-technical challenges to guide future research.
papers.conclusion: The review outlines critical open problems in mechanistic interpretability that must be addressed to achieve scientific and engineering goals, emphasizing the need for methodological improvements and socio-technical integration.
papers.key_findings:
Mechanistic interpretability methods, such as sparse dictionary learning, suffer from practical and conceptual limitations like high reconstruction errors and unclear theoretical foundations.
Applying interpretability to AI safety requires robust methods for monitoring internal states and controlling behavior, but current techniques are insufficient.
Socio-technical challenges include integrating interpretability into AI governance and addressing philosophical questions about the field's goals.
future_direction: Developing better decomposition methods like sparse dictionary learning with lower reconstruction errors.
Creating validation frameworks for interpretability hypotheses.
Applying interpretability to AI safety monitoring and control.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to understand the computational mechanisms underlying neural networks' capabilities in order to accomplish concrete scientific and engineering goals. Progress in this field thus promises to provide greater assurance over AI system behavior and shed light on exciting scientific questions about the nature of intelligence. Despite recent progress toward these goals, there are many open problems in the field that require solutions before many scientific and practical benefits can be realized: Our methods require both conceptual and practical improvements to reveal deeper insights; we must figure out how best to apply our methods in pursuit of specific goals; and the field must grapple with socio-technical challenges that influence and are influenced by our work. This forward-facing review discusses the current frontier of mechanistic interpretability and the open problems that the field may benefit from prioritizing.

papers.title: Interpretability for Time Series Transformers using A Concept Bottleneck Framework
papers.research_question: How can we make time series transformers interpretable by steering them to learn predefined, interpretable concepts while maintaining forecasting performance?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a training framework based on Concept Bottleneck Models and Centered Kernel Alignment to steer time series transformers to learn predefined interpretable concepts (e.g., a linear surrogate model and time features) in a designated bottleneck layer, improving interpretability without significantly harming forecasting performance.
papers.conclusion: The concept bottleneck framework successfully improves the interpretability of time series transformers by encouraging specific components to align with human-understandable concepts, with minimal impact on forecasting accuracy, and enables faithful local interventions.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed framework maintains model performance (MSE, MAE) on benchmark datasets while making the bottleneck layer's representations highly similar to the predefined concepts, as measured by CKA.
Component visualizations and activation patching interventions confirm that the bottleneck components learn and causally influence the model's predictions based on the intended concepts.
The framework is successfully applied to three different transformer architectures (Vanilla Transformer, Autoformer, FEDformer) on synthetic and real-world time series data.
Including a 'free' component in the bottleneck (not constrained by concepts) can help maintain performance and capture additional, non-predefined patterns in the data.
The intervention experiment demonstrates that the model's performance on time-shifted data can be restored by patching the activations of the time-concept component, confirming the causal role of the bottleneck.
papers.limitation:
The method assumes that relevant, interpretable concepts are known a priori and provided to the model.
The framework introduces additional computational cost during training due to the CKA loss calculation.
future_direction: Extending the framework to other types of sequential data beyond time series.
Exploring more complex or domain-specific interpretable concepts.
Investigating the use of the framework for model debugging and out-of-distribution robustness.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability focuses on reverse engineering the internal mechanisms learned by neural networks. We extend our focus and propose to mechanistically forward engineer using our framework based on Concept Bottleneck Models. In the context of long-term time series forecasting, we modify the training objective to encourage a model to develop representations which are similar to predefined, interpretable concepts using Centered Kernel Alignment. This steers the bottleneck components to learn the predefined concepts, while allowing other components to learn other, undefined concepts. We apply the framework to the Vanilla Transformer, Autoformer and FEDformer, and present an in-depth analysis on synthetic data and on a variety of benchmark datasets. We find that the model performance remains mostly unaffected, while the model shows much improved interpretability. Additionally, we verify the interpretation of the bottleneck components with an intervention experiment using activation patching.

papers.title: Linear Latent World Models in Simple Transformers: A Case Study on Othello-GPT
papers.research_question: How does Othello-GPT encode and utilize a linear world model for decision-making in the game of Othello?
papers.core_contribution: Othello-GPT encodes a linear representation of the board state in its activations, and this representation is causally utilized for next-move predictions, with the world model finalized in middle layers.
papers.conclusion: Othello-GPT neurons encode board state information linearly, and this representation is used causally for decision-making in deep networks, with the world model finalized in middle layers.
papers.key_findings:
Othello-GPT linearly encodes board state information in its activations, with accuracy increasing in deeper layers.
Causal interventions demonstrate that the linear world model is used for next-move predictions, particularly in middle layers.
Attention heads can be categorized into types such as 'my token' and 'their token' heads, which track player moves.
Even 1-layer models can encode linear board states, but only deeper models use this information causally for decision-making.
The linear world model is fully developed in middle layers, and later layers may rely on surface statistics.
papers.limitation: Causal interventions are only successful in middle layers and early games, and may not apply to late games where the model might rely on surface statistics.
future_direction: Using mechanistic interpretability tools to understand circuits and decision-making in Othello-GPT.
papers.abstract: Foundation models exhibit significant capabilities in decision-making and logical deductions. Nonetheless, a continuing discourse persists regarding their genuine understanding of the world as opposed to mere stochastic mimicry. This paper meticulously examines a simple transformer trained for Othello, extending prior research to enhance comprehension of the emergent world model of Othello-GPT. The investigation reveals that Othello-GPT encapsulates a linear representation of opposing pieces, a factor that causally steers its decision-making process. This paper further elucidates the interplay between the linear world representation and causal decision-making, and their dependence on layer depth and model complexity. We have made the code public.

papers.title: Universal Redundancies in Time Series Foundation Models
papers.research_question: What mechanisms enable TSFMs to construct effective zero-shot forecasts?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds universal redundancies in Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs), shows that middle layers are highly redundant and models are robust to ablations, and introduces an intrinsic head-pruning strategy based on stable rank to identify heads responsible for context parroting and seasonality bias.
papers.conclusion: The study sheds light on universal properties of TSFMs, revealing redundancies and providing an intrinsic head-pruning strategy that identifies heads responsible for common failure modes.
papers.key_findings:
Middle layers in TSFMs are highly redundant and can be ablated with minimal performance drop.
An intrinsic head pruning strategy based on the stable rank of query-key projection matrices effectively identifies important heads.
Specific attention heads are responsible for degenerate phenomena such as context parroting and seasonality bias.
TSFMs exhibit significant variation in sensitivity to MLP ablations across architectures, with encoder-decoder models being more resilient.
The first and last layers are most important for model performance.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical framework is technically limited to encoder-decoder models with causal masking.
The intrinsic head pruning strategy cannot account for the data-dependent exponential tilt term in the attention mechanism.
future_direction: Investigating how architecture determines what the transformer loads onto MLPs versus attention heads.
papers.abstract: Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) leverage extensive pretraining to accurately predict unseen time series during inference, without the need for task-specific fine-tuning. Through large-scale evaluations on standard benchmarks, we find that leading transformer-based TSFMs exhibit redundant components in their intermediate layers. We introduce a set of tools for mechanistic interpretability of TSFMs, including ablations of specific components and direct logit attribution on the residual stream. Our findings are consistent across several leading TSFMs with diverse architectures, and across a diverse set of real-world and synthetic time-series datasets. We discover that all models in our study are robust to ablations of entire layers. Furthermore, we develop a theoretical framework framing transformers as kernel regressors, motivating a purely intrinsic strategy for ablating heads based on the stable rank of the per-head projection matrices. Using this approach, we uncover the specific heads responsible for degenerate phenomena widely observed in TSFMs, such as parroting of motifs from the context and seasonality bias. Our study sheds light on the universal properties of this emerging class of architectures for continuous-time sequence modeling.

papers.title: time2time: Causal Intervention in Hidden States to Simulate Rare Events in Time Series Foundation Models
papers.research_question: Do time series foundation models internalize semantic concepts like market regimes, and can their internal representations be leveraged to simulate rare events such as market crashes?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces activation transplantation, a causal intervention method that provides evidence that time series foundation models learn high-level semantic concepts of real-world events, enabling steerable simulations for stress-testing.
papers.conclusion: The paper provides causal evidence that time series foundation models encode abstract, steerable market regime concepts, enabling deterministic control of forecasts and revealing a continuous severity axis in their latent representations.
papers.key_findings:
Activation transplantation can deterministically steer forecasts by implanting the statistical signature of one event into another.
Models encode event severity as a continuous latent variable, with the activation vector norm correlating with shock magnitude.
The steerable representations are robust across different model architectures (decoder-only Toto and encoder-decoder Chronos).
A unified 'crash' concept emerges across layers, with early layers showing anti-correlation and later layers converging to a shared subspace.
The model's internal representation of a crash is not binary but continuous, allowing for graded interventions.
papers.limitation: The work is a foundational proof-of-concept and it remains to be investigated whether steerable semantic subspaces are universal beyond Transformers to other architectures like State Space Models or LSTMs.
future_direction: Investigate whether steerable semantic subspaces are universal across sequence models beyond Transformers, such as State Space Models and LSTMs.
Discover a broader semantic vocabulary within TSFMs, probing for concepts like earnings surprises in finance or seizure onsets in EEG data.
papers.abstract: While transformer-based foundation models excel at forecasting routine patterns, two questions remain: do they internalize semantic concepts such as market regimes, or merely fit curves? And can their internal representations be leveraged to simulate rare, high-stakes events such as market crashes? To investigate this, we introduce activation transplantation, a causal intervention that manipulates hidden states by imposing the statistical moments of one event (e.g., a historical crash) onto another (e.g., a calm period) during the forward pass. This procedure deterministically steers forecasts: injecting crash semantics induces downturn predictions, while injecting calm semantics suppresses crashes and restores stability. Beyond binary control, we find that models encode a graded notion of event severity, with the latent vector norm directly correlating with the magnitude of systemic shocks. Validated across two architecturally distinct TSFMs, Toto (decoder only) and Chronos (encoder-decoder), our results demonstrate that steerable, semantically grounded representations are a robust property of large time series transformers. Our findings provide evidence for a latent concept space that governs model predictions, shifting interpretability from post-hoc attribution to direct causal intervention, and enabling semantic "what-if" analysis for strategic stress-testing.

papers.title: Enhancing Multimodal Large Language Models Complex Reason via Similarity Computation
papers.research_question: How can the complex reasoning ability of Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) be improved by efficiently utilizing image information and filtering out irrelevant image tokens?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that image tokens semantically related to text have information flow convergence and higher attention scores in the LLM decoder, and proposes Simignore, a method to filter irrelevant image tokens based on similarity computation, which improves complex reasoning performance.
papers.conclusion: The proposed Simignore method, which computes similarity between image and text embeddings to filter irrelevant tokens, enhances the complex reasoning ability of LVLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Image tokens semantically related to text prompts are more likely to have information flow convergence and receive higher attention scores in the LLM decoder.
Filtering out irrelevant image tokens based on similarity between image and text embeddings improves the accuracy of LVLMs on complex reasoning tasks.
The performance improvement depends on the number of tokens ignored, with an optimal number (e.g., 124 out of 576 for LLaVA1.5-7B) yielding the best results.
Important image tokens (with high similarity to text) are crucial for complex reasoning, while unimportant tokens can be ignored to improve performance and reduce computation.
Cosine similarity performs better than Euclidean and Manhattan distance for computing the similarity between image and text embeddings in this task.
papers.limitation:
The method does not adaptively choose the number of image tokens to ignore.
The internal mechanisms of how image and textual information work together to facilitate complex reasoning are not fully understood.
future_direction: Exploring strategies for adaptively choosing the number of image tokens to ignore.
Investigating the internal mechanisms of the model to more fully understand how image and textual information work together.
papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models have experienced rapid growth, and numerous different models have emerged. The interpretability of LVLMs remains an under-explored area. Especially when faced with more complex tasks such as chain-of-thought reasoning, its internal mechanisms still resemble a black box that is difficult to decipher. By studying the interaction and information flow between images and text, we noticed that in models such as LLaVA1.5, image tokens that are semantically related to text are more likely to have information flow convergence in the LLM decoding layer, and these image tokens receive higher attention scores. However, those image tokens that are less relevant to the text do not have information flow convergence, and they only get very small attention scores. To efficiently utilize the image information, we propose a new image token reduction method, Simignore, which aims to improve the complex reasoning ability of LVLMs by computing the similarity between image and text embeddings and ignoring image tokens that are irrelevant and unimportant to the text. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our method for complex reasoning tasks.

papers.title: DLM-Scope: Mechanistic Interpretability of Diffusion Language Models via Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders (SAEs) be used for mechanistic interpretability in diffusion language models (DLMs), and how do their properties and applications differ from those in autoregressive LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DLM-Scope, the first SAE-based interpretability framework for Diffusion Language Models (DLMs), demonstrating that SAEs can extract interpretable features, enable effective diffusion-time steering, analyze decoding order, and transfer from base to instruction-tuned models.
papers.conclusion: DLM-Scope establishes a foundation for mechanistic interpretability in DLMs and shows the great potential of applying SAEs to DLM-related tasks and algorithms.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs trained on DLMs achieve a favorable sparsity-fidelity trade-off and can even reduce cross-entropy loss when inserted in early layers, a phenomenon absent or weaker in LLMs.
SAE features enable effective diffusion-time interventions (steering) that often outperform single-pass LLM steering.
SAE feature dynamics provide a useful signal for analyzing and correlating with the performance of different DLM decoding-order strategies.
Base-trained SAEs transfer almost losslessly to instruction-tuned DLMs in shallow and middle layers, but not in the deepest layer, indicating tuning-specific changes in deep representations.
future_direction: As DLMs scale, we plan to extend SAEs to more DLMs to better understand and improve models.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have become a standard tool for mechanistic interpretability in autoregressive large language models (LLMs), enabling researchers to extract sparse, human-interpretable features and intervene on model behavior. Recently, as diffusion language models (DLMs) have become an increasingly promising alternative to the autoregressive LLMs, it is essential to develop tailored mechanistic interpretability tools for this emerging class of models. In this work, we present DLM-Scope, the first SAE-based interpretability framework for DLMs, and demonstrate that trained Top-K SAEs can faithfully extract interpretable features. Notably, we find that inserting SAEs affects DLMs differently than autoregressive LLMs: while SAE insertion in LLMs typically incurs a loss penalty, in DLMs it can reduce cross-entropy loss when applied to early layers, a phenomenon absent or markedly weaker in LLMs. Additionally, SAE features in DLMs enable more effective diffusion-time interventions, often outperforming LLM steering. Moreover, we pioneer certain new SAE-based research directions for DLMs: we show that SAEs can provide useful signals for DLM decoding order; and the SAE features are stable during the post-training phase of DLMs. Our work establishes a foundation for mechanistic interpretability in DLMs and shows a great potential of applying SAEs to DLM-related tasks and algorithms.

papers.title: Unveiling the Mystery of Weight in Large Foundation Models: Gaussian Distribution Never Fades
papers.research_question: What are the distributional properties of weights in large foundation models, and how can these properties be leveraged to simplify model adaptation and editing?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers that weights in large foundation models follow a Gaussian distribution and that transformation weights can be derived from Gaussian noise, leading to a method that improves adaptation and editing by adjusting the standard deviation of the noise and updating outliers.
papers.conclusion: The Gaussian distribution of weights is a fundamental property that can be leveraged to simplify adaptation and editing, and optimal weights are sparse with a Gaussian-like distribution.
papers.key_findings:
Pre-trained weights of LFMs predominantly follow a Gaussian distribution.
Transformation weights (∆W) can be derived from Gaussian noise and primarily increase the standard deviation of pre-trained weights.
The standard deviation of transformation weights grows with layer depth.
Optimal weights should exhibit zero-mean, symmetry, and sparsity, with sparse values following a truncated Gaussian distribution and a few outliers.
Adaptation and editing can be improved by adjusting Gaussian signals and outliers.
papers.abstract: This paper presents a pioneering exploration of the mechanisms underlying large foundation models' (LFMs) weights, aiming to simplify AI research. Through extensive observation and analysis on prevailing LFMs, we find that regardless of initialization strategies, their weights predominantly follow a Gaussian distribution, with occasional sharp, inverted T-shaped, or linear patterns. We further discover that the weights share the i.i.d. properties of Gaussian noise, and explore their direct relationship. We find that transformation weights can be derived from Gaussian noise, and they primarily serve to increase the standard deviation of pre-trained weights, with their standard deviation growing with layer depth. In other words, transformation weights broaden the acceptable deviation from the optimal weights, facilitating adaptation to downstream tasks. Building upon the above conclusions, we thoroughly discussed the nature of optimal weights, ultimately concluding that they should exhibit zero-mean, symmetry, and sparsity, with the sparse values being a truncated Gaussian distribution and a few outliers. Our experiments in LFM adaptation and editing demonstrate the effectiveness of these insights. We hope these findings can provide a foundational understanding to pave the way for future advancements in the LFM community.

papers.title: Enhancing Automated Interpretability with Output-Centric Feature Descriptions
papers.research_question: How can we generate faithful feature descriptions for LLMs by considering both the inputs that activate a feature and its causal effect on model outputs?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes efficient, output-centric methods (VocabProj and TokenChange) for automatically generating feature descriptions in LLMs, and demonstrates that combining these with input-centric methods yields the most faithful descriptions across both input and output evaluations.
papers.conclusion: Output-centric methods provide efficient and effective ways to generate feature descriptions that capture causal effects, and their combination with input-centric methods yields more faithful and complete descriptions, enhancing automated interpretability pipelines.
papers.key_findings:
Output-centric feature descriptions (VocabProj, TokenChange) better capture the causal effect of a feature on model outputs than the prevalent input-centric method (MaxAct).
Combining input- and output-centric methods (ensembles) leads to the best performance on both input- and output-based evaluations of description faithfulness.
Output-centric methods are computationally efficient, requiring only a few inference passes, and can serve as a cheap alternative to MaxAct in some cases.
Output-centric descriptions can be used to find inputs that activate 'dead' features for which no activating inputs were previously identified.
Performance varies by layer and feature type, with output-based performance being lower for MLP features compared to residual stream features.
papers.abstract: Automated interpretability pipelines generate natural language descriptions for the concepts represented by features in large language models (LLMs), such as plants or the first word in a sentence. These descriptions are derived using inputs that activate the feature, which may be a dimension or a direction in the model's representation space. However, identifying activating inputs is costly, and the mechanistic role of a feature in model behavior is determined both by how inputs cause a feature to activate and by how feature activation affects outputs. Using steering evaluations, we reveal that current pipelines provide descriptions that fail to capture the causal effect of the feature on outputs. To fix this, we propose efficient, output-centric methods for automatically generating feature descriptions. These methods use the tokens weighted higher after feature stimulation or the highest weight tokens after applying the vocabulary "unembedding" head directly to the feature. Our output-centric descriptions better capture the causal effect of a feature on model outputs than input-centric descriptions, but combining the two leads to the best performance on both input and output evaluations. Lastly, we show that output-centric descriptions can be used to find inputs that activate features previously thought to be "dead".
