papers.title: Scale Alone Does not Improve Mechanistic Interpretability in Vision Models
papers.research_question: Does scaling model and dataset size improve the mechanistic interpretability of vision models at the level of individual units?
papers.core_contribution: Scaling model and dataset size does not improve the mechanistic interpretability of vision models at the level of individual units, and latest-generation models may even be less interpretable than older ones.
papers.conclusion: Scale alone does not improve mechanistic interpretability in vision models; explicit design for interpretability is needed, and the released dataset can facilitate research on automated interpretability measures.
papers.key_findings:
No practically relevant differences in interpretability across nine vision models of varying scales, indicating that scaling does not improve interpretability.
Feature visualizations are less helpful than natural exemplars for explaining unit activations across all models, including adversarially robust models.
Interpretability does not increase with model classification performance or human-likeness, and may even decrease for feature visualizations as accuracy increases.
For models pre-trained on large datasets (Clip ResNet and Clip ViT), later layers are more interpretable, suggesting a shift in interpretability across layers.
Interpretability drops sharply when the task difficulty increases slightly, indicating that human understanding of unit behavior is limited.
papers.limitation:
The study only employed two widely-used explanation methods (feature visualizations and natural exemplars), which may not capture all aspects of interpretability.
Feature visualizations for ViT models were not evaluated due to methodological challenges, limiting the comparison for transformer architectures.
future_direction: Designing models explicitly for interpretability rather than relying on scale.
Developing automated interpretability measures using the released dataset to avoid costly human evaluations.
Further research on interpretability methods beyond feature visualizations and natural exemplars.
papers.abstract: In light of the recent widespread adoption of AI systems, understanding the internal information processing of neural networks has become increasingly critical. Most recently, machine vision has seen remarkable progress by scaling neural networks to unprecedented levels in dataset and model size. We here ask whether this extraordinary increase in scale also positively impacts the field of mechanistic interpretability. In other words, has our understanding of the inner workings of scaled neural networks improved as well? We use a psychophysical paradigm to quantify one form of mechanistic interpretability for a diverse suite of nine models and find no scaling effect for interpretability - neither for model nor dataset size. Specifically, none of the investigated state-of-the-art models are easier to interpret than the GoogLeNet model from almost a decade ago. Latest-generation vision models appear even less interpretable than older architectures, hinting at a regression rather than improvement, with modern models sacrificing interpretability for accuracy. These results highlight the need for models explicitly designed to be mechanistically interpretable and the need for more helpful interpretability methods to increase our understanding of networks at an atomic level. We release a dataset containing more than 130'000 human responses from our psychophysical evaluation of 767 units across nine models. This dataset facilitates research on automated instead of human-based interpretability evaluations, which can ultimately be leveraged to directly optimize the mechanistic interpretability of models.

papers.title: Model Interpretability through the Lens of Computational Complexity
papers.research_question: How can we formally compare the interpretability of different model classes using computational complexity theory?
papers.core_contribution: The paper develops a complexity-based framework (c-interpretability) for comparing model interpretability and proves that it aligns with folklore beliefs: linear and tree-based models are more interpretable than neural networks, and shallow networks are more interpretable than deep ones.
papers.conclusion: The complexity-based framework provides a formal correlate to folklore interpretability claims, but the authors do not claim it as the definitive notion of interpretability, which remains subjective.
papers.key_findings:
FBDDs are strictly more c-interpretable than MLPs with respect to the minimum change required (MCR), minimum sufficient reason (MSR), and count completions (CC) queries.
Perceptrons are strictly more c-interpretable than MLPs for MCR and MSR, but not for CC, where both are #P-complete.
The comparison between FBDDs and perceptrons is mixed: perceptrons are more c-interpretable for MSR, while FBDDs are more c-interpretable for CC; both are in PTIME for MCR.
Using parameterized complexity, the paper shows that shallow MLPs are more interpretable than deeper MLPs for the MCR query.
The complexity of answering explainability queries varies across model classes: for example, MCR is in PTIME for FBDDs and perceptrons but NP-complete for MLPs.
papers.abstract: In spite of several claims stating that some models are more interpretable than others -- e.g., "linear models are more interpretable than deep neural networks" -- we still lack a principled notion of interpretability to formally compare among different classes of models. We make a step towards such a notion by studying whether folklore interpretability claims have a correlate in terms of computational complexity theory. We focus on local post-hoc explainability queries that, intuitively, attempt to answer why individual inputs are classified in a certain way by a given model. In a nutshell, we say that a class $\mathcal{C}_1$ of models is more interpretable than another class $\mathcal{C}_2$, if the computational complexity of answering post-hoc queries for models in $\mathcal{C}_2$ is higher than for those in $\mathcal{C}_1$. We prove that this notion provides a good theoretical counterpart to current beliefs on the interpretability of models; in particular, we show that under our definition and assuming standard complexity-theoretical assumptions (such as P$\neq$NP), both linear and tree-based models are strictly more interpretable than neural networks. Our complexity analysis, however, does not provide a clear-cut difference between linear and tree-based models, as we obtain different results depending on the particular post-hoc explanations considered. Finally, by applying a finer complexity analysis based on parameterized complexity, we are able to prove a theoretical result suggesting that shallow neural networks are more interpretable than deeper ones.

papers.title: Does TabPFN Understand Causal Structures?
papers.research_question: Does TabPFN, a transformer-based tabular foundation model, encode causal knowledge in its internal representations beyond statistical correlations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that TabPFN's embeddings contain causal information, and introduces an adapter framework that can extract this information for causal discovery, outperforming traditional statistical methods.
papers.conclusion: TabPFN's embeddings contain causal information, and the proposed adapter framework can extract this information for causal discovery, establishing a new direction for interpretable and adaptable tabular foundation models.
papers.key_findings:
Causal information is concentrated in the middle layers (4-6) of TabPFN's encoder.
The proposed framework extracts causal signals from TabPFN's frozen embeddings and outperforms statistical baselines (GIES, IGSP, DCDI) on ROC AUC, performing closely to the specialized neural causal discovery model A VICI.
The decoder architecture is crucial for performance; using a learnable decoder significantly improves results compared to using no decoder.
Performance degrades with increasing feature sizes, particularly for dense graph structures like Erdős-Rényi and Stochastic Block Model graphs.
Using embeddings from the pre-trained TabPFN encoder (optimal weights) yields better causal discovery performance than using randomly initialized or degraded encoder weights.
papers.limitation: Performance degrades with increasing feature sizes, and the approach is sensitive to the type of graph structure.
future_direction: Leveraging pre-trained tabular models for extracting causal structures and improving their interpretability.
Understanding how tabular foundation models reason about different datasets.
Repurposing tabular foundation models for different downstream tasks.
papers.abstract: Causal discovery is fundamental for multiple scientific domains, yet extracting causal information from real world data remains a significant challenge. Given the recent success on real data, we investigate whether TabPFN, a transformer-based tabular foundation model pre-trained on synthetic datasets generated from structural causal models, encodes causal information in its internal representations. We develop an adapter framework using a learnable decoder and causal tokens that extract causal signals from TabPFN's frozen embeddings and decode them into adjacency matrices for causal discovery. Our evaluations demonstrate that TabPFN's embeddings contain causal information, outperforming several traditional causal discovery algorithms, with such causal information being concentrated in mid-range layers. These findings establish a new direction for interpretable and adaptable foundation models and demonstrate the potential for leveraging pre-trained tabular models for causal discovery.

papers.title: TabPFN Through The Looking Glass: An interpretability study of TabPFN and its internal representations
papers.research_question: How does TabPFN, a tabular foundational model, process and transform input features? What information is encoded in its hidden representations and how do these representations evolve across layers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides evidence that TabPFN encodes intermediate and final quantities of simple arithmetic tasks in its hidden representations in a linearly decodable manner, suggesting the model performs structured, hierarchical computation internally.
papers.conclusion: TabPFN implements systematic, hierarchical computation, with intermediate results linearly represented in the residual stream, moving towards more interpretable and trustworthy tabular foundation models.
papers.key_findings:
Linear regression coefficients can be linearly decoded from the model's hidden states within a single model fit, but not across different fits.
Intermediate arithmetic terms (e.g., a*b) are linearly decodable from middle-layer activations, indicating the model respects the order of operations.
The final answer can be decoded from hidden states earlier in the network (layer 5) than it is correctly projected to the output space via the logit lens (layer 8).
Input values and their linear combinations can be decoded from the activations of the answer token early in the model, suggesting a copying mechanism.
The model does not maintain a fixed, universal encoding of coefficients across different fits; representations are fit-specific.
papers.limitation: The analysis is limited to simple arithmetic (additive/multiplicative) toy expressions, unlike the highly complex, noisy functions found in real-world datasets.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to more complex, real-world functions.
Using mechanistic interpretability methods like activation patching to find the mechanisms through which the answer is computed.
Manipulating the function through steering vectors or vector ablation.
papers.abstract: Tabular foundational models are pre-trained models designed for a wide range of tabular data tasks. They have shown strong performance across domains, yet their internal representations and learned concepts remain poorly understood. This lack of interpretability makes it important to study how these models process and transform input features. In this work, we analyze the information encoded inside the model's hidden representations and examine how these representations evolve across layers. We run a set of probing experiments that test for the presence of linear regression coefficients, intermediate values from complex expressions, and the final answer in early layers. These experiments allow us to reason about the computations the model performs internally. Our results provide evidence that meaningful and structured information is stored inside the representations of tabular foundational models. We observe clear signals that correspond to both intermediate and final quantities involved in the model's prediction process. This gives insight into how the model refines its inputs and how the final output emerges. Our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the internal mechanics of tabular foundational models. They show that these models encode concrete and interpretable information, which moves us closer to making their decision processes more transparent and trustworthy.

papers.title: The Mythos of Model Interpretability
papers.research_question: What are the motivations for interpretability in machine learning, and what properties or techniques are thought to confer interpretability to models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a critical analysis of the concept of interpretability in machine learning, arguing that the term is ill-defined and encompasses diverse and sometimes conflicting motivations and notions, and that claims about interpretability must be qualified with specific definitions.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that the machine learning community must critically engage with the problem formulation of interpretability, and that researchers and practitioners share responsibility for ensuring machine learning aligns with societal desiderata.
papers.key_findings:
Linear models are not strictly more interpretable than deep neural networks; the validity of such a claim depends on the specific notion of interpretability being used (e.g., algorithmic transparency vs. decomposability).
Claims about interpretability must be qualified by specifying the definition of interpretability being employed, as the term refers to multiple distinct concepts.
In some cases, the desire for model transparency may conflict with broader objectives of AI, such as achieving higher predictive performance.
Post-hoc interpretations can potentially mislead, especially if they are optimized to produce plausible but unfaithful explanations.
The demand for interpretability often arises from a mismatch between formal machine learning objectives (e.g., test set performance) and real-world deployment costs or desiderata.
future_direction: Developing richer loss functions and performance metrics to mitigate the discrepancy between real-life and machine learning objectives.
Expanding the analysis of interpretability to other machine learning paradigms such as reinforcement learning.
Addressing challenges like fairness and contestability in the context of interpretability.
papers.abstract: In machine learning, the concept of interpretability is both important and slippery.

papers.title: MechIR: A Mechanistic Interpretability Framework for Information Retrieval
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MechIR, a flexible framework for mechanistic interpretability analysis and intervention in neural information retrieval models.
papers.conclusion: MechIR provides a framework to make mechanistic interpretability accessible for IR, enabling diagnostic analysis and interventions for neural retrieval models.
papers.key_findings:
Bi-encoders show diffuse activation patterns with no single head strongly responding to query term addition, and early layers penalize term addition.
Cross-encoders have consistent head activations under term matching, primarily in final layers with some in middle layers.
The framework enables causal interventions to isolate and modify model behaviors, such as reducing penalization of salient terms in bi-encoders.
papers.limitation: The observed penalization in early layers of bi-encoders may be an artifact of term matching or positional bias, requiring further investigation.
future_direction: Extend MechIR to support additional mechanistic interpretability methods like path patching.
Apply the framework to other areas of IR like recommender systems.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability is an emerging diagnostic approach for neural models that has gained traction in broader natural language processing domains. This paradigm aims to provide attribution to components of neural systems where causal relationships between hidden layers and output were previously uninterpretable. As the use of neural models in IR for retrieval and evaluation becomes ubiquitous, we need to ensure that we can interpret why a model produces a given output for both transparency and the betterment of systems. This work comprises a flexible framework for diagnostic analysis and intervention within these highly parametric neural systems specifically tailored for IR tasks and architectures. In providing such a framework, we look to facilitate further research in interpretable IR with a broader scope for practical interventions derived from mechanistic interpretability. We provide preliminary analysis and look to demonstrate our framework through an axiomatic lens to show its applications and ease of use for those IR practitioners inexperienced in this emerging paradigm.

papers.title: On the Semantic Interpretability of Artificial Intelligence Models
papers.research_question: What is semantic interpretability in AI models, and how do different AI fields (beyond machine learning) approach and implement interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a broad survey of semantic interpretability across AI fields, categorizing models into data, algorithmic, and hybrid types, and analyzing how they introduce interpretability features and their impact on users.
papers.conclusion: Interpretability is a crucial, cross-disciplinary challenge in AI; while progress has been made, more work is needed to provide user-friendly, integrated interpretability solutions for a wide range of models without compromising performance.
papers.key_findings:
Interpretability is a cross-field AI concern, not exclusive to machine learning, encompassing areas like distributional semantics and fuzzy logic.
Models can be categorized as data models (e.g., interpretable DSMs), algorithmic models (e.g., fuzzy systems, decision sets), or hybrid models (e.g., topic models) based on their primary interpretability component.
Interpretability techniques are divided into transparency (simulatability, decomposability) and post-hoc explanations, with most models focusing on transparency.
The trade-off between interpretability and accuracy remains an issue, and interpretability layers offer a low-risk way to add explanations to existing systems.
Future work must shift from accuracy-only approaches to human-centered design to integrate interpretability seamlessly into user workflows.
papers.limitation: The paper is a survey and does not conduct empirical evaluations of the interpretability methods discussed.
future_direction: Developing human-centered model analysis, design, and implementation choices.
Integrating interpretability features (like post-hoc explanations) into user workflows without affecting current system results and procedures.
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence models are becoming increasingly more powerful and accurate, supporting or even replacing humans' decision making. But with increased power and accuracy also comes higher complexity, making it hard for users to understand how the model works and what the reasons behind its predictions are. Humans must explain and justify their decisions, and so do the AI models supporting them in this process, making semantic interpretability an emerging field of study. In this work, we look at interpretability from a broader point of view, going beyond the machine learning scope and covering different AI fields such as distributional semantics and fuzzy logic, among others. We examine and classify the models according to their nature and also based on how they introduce interpretability features, analyzing how each approach affects the final users and pointing to gaps that still need to be addressed to provide more human-centered interpretability solutions.

papers.title: MindCraft: How Concept Trees Take Shape In Deep Models
papers.research_question: How do neural networks internally construct and consolidate abstract concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the MindCraft framework and Concept Trees to systematically trace how abstract concepts emerge, branch, and stabilize across layers in deep models.
papers.conclusion: MindCraft provides a hierarchical reconstruction of a model's reasoning process, offering a significant step towards building transparent, interpretable, and accountable AI systems.
papers.key_findings:
Concept Trees reveal a hierarchical, tree-shaped organization of concept separation within models, with more salient concepts branching earlier.
The method captures conceptual importance shaped by context, not just token embedding distances.
Propagation patterns of counterfactual differences are consistent across diverse tasks, indicating a robust hierarchical dynamic.
Concept separation layers are disentangled from input embedding distances, highlighting the framework's ability to analyze high-level conceptual organization.
The framework is applicable across multiple model architectures and scales, demonstrating generality.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to multi-modal domains.
Using the identified Concept Paths to perform precise, surgical edits on model behavior.
Exploring the compositional 'algebra' of how multiple concepts interact within the network's learned representation space.
papers.abstract: Large-scale foundation models demonstrate strong performance across language, vision, and reasoning tasks. However, how they internally structure and stabilize concepts remains elusive. Inspired by causal inference, we introduce the MindCraft framework built upon Concept Trees. By applying spectral decomposition at each layer and linking principal directions into branching Concept Paths, Concept Trees reconstruct the hierarchical emergence of concepts, revealing exactly when they diverge from shared representations into linearly separable subspaces. Empirical evaluations across diverse scenarios across disciplines, including medical diagnosis, physics reasoning, and political decision-making, show that Concept Trees recover semantic hierarchies, disentangle latent concepts, and can be widely applied across multiple domains. The Concept Tree establishes a widely applicable and powerful framework that enables in-depth analysis of conceptual representations in deep models, marking a significant step forward in the foundation of interpretable AI.

papers.title: From Explanations to Interpretability and Back
papers.research_question: What are the connections between interpretability in machine learning and scientific/mathematical explanations, and how can we better understand interpretability through these connections?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a philosophical analysis that proposes to distinguish kinds of interpretability using the parts of ML we want to explain and the parts we use to explain (interpretability types), argues for a pluralistic and context-dependent view of interpretability, and highlights under-explored issues like theoretical explanations.
papers.conclusion: Viewing interpretability from the perspective of scientific and mathematical explanations is advantageous; it is preferable to convey the complexity and limits of our current knowledge rather than providing oversimplified, non-factive explanations.
papers.key_findings:
Interpretability can be classified into types based on the explanandum and explanans parts of ML (e.g., M ↦ ŷ).
Not all explanations are contrastive, and contrasts can be with respect to models and data, not just inputs.
Interpretability has a necessary context-dependence (audience, purpose) but radical context-dependence is problematic.
Theoretical explanations (e.g., for generalization, optimization, expressivity of DNNs) are an under-explored area.
Pluralism is advocated: there are different notions of interpretability and different notions of scientific/mathematical explanations, but their heterogeneity does not straightforwardly transfer.
papers.abstract: Abstract This chapter discusses connections between the interpretability of machine learning and (scientific and mathematical) explanations, provides novel perspectives on interpretability, and highlights under-explored issues. Interpretability types are proposed: kinds of interpretability should be distinguished using both the parts of ML we want to explain and the parts of ML we use to explain. It is argued that not all explanations are contrastive, and that we should also consider contrasts with respect to models and data, not only with respect to inputs. Theoretical explanations are highlighted; they include issues like generalization, optimization, and expressivity. It is proposed that there are two threats to the objectivity of explanations: One comes from radical subject-dependence, the other from a lack of factivity. Finally, pluralism is advocated: There are different notions of interpretability and different notions of (scientific and mathematical) explanations. However, the heterogeneity of one area does not transfer to the other in a straightforward manner.

papers.title: Data Science Principles for Interpretable and Explainable AI
papers.core_contribution: This review synthesizes key principles from the growing literature on interpretable and explainable AI, introducing vocabulary, connecting to classical principles, illustrating basic techniques with a case study, and outlining open challenges.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes by outlining open challenges in interpretable AI, including the need for human-centered evaluation, handling of multimodal data, and the development of techniques with formal guarantees, and discusses the potential role of data science in addressing them.
papers.key_findings:
Distinguishes between intrinsically interpretable (glass box) models and explainability techniques for black boxes.
Highlights core data science principles underlying interpretability: parsimony, simulatability, sensitivity, navigating scales, and interaction gulfs.
Illustrates that simple models on appropriate representations can achieve good performance, challenging a strict interpretability-accuracy tradeoff.
Emphasizes that interpretability must be tailored to the audience and their goals, and that evaluation requires realistic settings.
Notes that explainability techniques like integrated gradients can be sensitive to implementation choices and lack formal guarantees.
future_direction: Developing human-centered evaluation frameworks for interpretability methods.
Creating interpretability techniques for multimodal and foundation models.
Establishing formal guarantees for local explainability methods.
Addressing the scalability of interpretability methods to very large models.
papers.abstract: Society’s capacity for algorithmic problem-solving has never been greater. Artificial Intelligence is now applied across more domains than ever, a consequence of powerful abstractions, abundant data, and accessible software. As capabilities have expanded, so have risks, with models often deployed without fully understanding their potential impacts. Interpretable and interactive machine learning aims to make complex models more transparent and controllable, enhancing user agency. This review synthesizes key principles from the growing literature in this field. We first introduce precise vocabulary for discussing interpretability, like the distinction between glass box and explainable models. We then explore connections to classical statistical and design principles, like parsimony and the gulfs of interaction. Basic explainability techniques – including learned embeddings, integrated gradients, and concept bottlenecks – are illustrated with a simple case study. We also review criteria for objectively evaluating interpretability approaches. Throughout, we underscore the importance of considering audience goals when designing interactive data-driven systems. Finally, we outline open challenges and discuss the potential role of data science in addressing them. Code to reproduce all examples can be found at https://go.wisc.edu/3k1ewe.

papers.title: Model learning with personalized interpretability estimation (ML-PIE)
papers.research_question: How can we synthesize models that are interpretable according to a specific user's subjective notion of interpretability by incorporating user feedback into the model synthesis process?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces ML-PIE, a human-in-the-loop active learning approach that synthesizes models with user-tailored interpretability by learning a personalized interpretability estimator from user feedback during the model synthesis process.
papers.conclusion: ML-PIE is a promising approach for synthesizing models with personalized interpretability, potentially advancing the field of explainable AI for high-stakes applications.
papers.key_findings:
ML-PIE can learn user-specific estimations of interpretability that can differ substantially across users.
The interpretability estimator in ML-PIE behaves sensibly, with low uncertainty and misprediction rates.
For more complex models, users tend to prefer models discovered by ML-PIE over those found using non-personalized interpretability indices (𝜙 and ℓ).
For simpler models, the choice of interpretability index does not significantly affect user preference.
The search performance of GP using the personalized estimator is not excessively harmed by the noise in the estimator.
papers.limitation:
The study did not involve actual domain experts and used a general set of model features for interpretability estimation.
The pace of user feedback may be too slow compared to the model synthesis process, which could harm the synthesis.
future_direction: Involve domain experts and add more specialized model features to the interpretability estimator.
Adapt ML-PIE to other model types (e.g., decision trees) and other model synthesis processes (e.g., reinforcement learning).
Study concurrency aspects, such as whether the model synthesis process should be halted based on the uncertainty of the interpretability estimator.
papers.abstract: High-stakes applications require AI-generated models to be interpretable. Current algorithms for the synthesis of potentially interpretable models rely on objectives or regularization terms that represent interpretability only coarsely (e.g., model size) and are not designed for a specific user. Yet, interpretability is intrinsically subjective. In this paper, we propose an approach for the synthesis of models that are tailored to the user by enabling the user to steer the model synthesis process according to her or his preferences. We use a bi-objective evolutionary algorithm to synthesize models with trade-offs between accuracy and a user-specific notion of interpretability. The latter is estimated by a neural network that is trained concurrently to the evolution using the feedback of the user, which is collected using uncertainty-based active learning. To maximize usability, the user is only asked to tell, given two models at the time, which one is less complex. With experiments on two real-world datasets involving 61 participants, we find that our approach is capable of learning estimations of interpretability that can be very different for different users. Moreover, the users tend to prefer models found using the proposed approach over models found using non-personalized interpretability indices.

papers.title: eDIF: A European Deep Inference Fabric for Remote Interpretability of LLM
papers.research_question: Can an NDIF-compatible infrastructure be effectively deployed under European institutional, funding, and regulatory conditions, and how well does such a system support real-world interpretability workflows by academic users?
papers.core_contribution: This feasibility study demonstrates the viability and research value of a European NDIF-compatible interpretability cluster (eDIF), successfully supporting remote, structured interventions on large models and facilitating reproducible experimentation for a diverse group of researchers.
papers.conclusion: The study establishes a solid foundation for scaling eDIF into a pan-European resource, fostering interdisciplinary collaboration and supporting the growing need for transparent, accessible AI systems.
papers.key_findings:
The eDIF system architecture proved stable and scalable, successfully provisioning models up to DeepSeek-R1-70B and supporting remote experimentation via the NNsight API.
User engagement increased steadily throughout the study, with high satisfaction ratings for onboarding and ease of use, and users reported significant time savings (10-50%) compared to local setups.
Technical challenges included prolonged download durations for activation data, intermittent execution interruptions, and inefficient GPU memory allocation due to an inability to share GPUs across models.
Migration experiments to an AMD-based HPC cluster demonstrated the general feasibility of operating NDIF on ROCm instead of CUDA, though structural challenges like Docker incompatibility and HPC scheduling constraints were encountered.
The study established a foundation for scaling eDIF into a pan-European resource, with strong user interest in sustained access and future developments like no-code interfaces and expanded model offerings.
papers.limitation:
Prolonged download durations for activation data and intermittent execution interruptions.
Absence of automatic GPU requirement estimation, requiring manual trial-and-error tuning for model deployments.
Inability to share GPUs across multiple models led to memory inefficiencies and a gap between theoretical GPU availability and effective resource utilization.
Docker-based setup was incompatible with HPC environments due to root access restrictions, requiring a partial migration to Apptainer which lacks full feature parity.
future_direction: Expanding the model repository to include modern, compact architectures such as Qwen and Gemma3, and enabling hot-swapping between models.
Developing no-code and low-code interfaces (e.g., visual tools, modular functional abstractions) to broaden accessibility and improve usability.
Establishing robust governance mechanisms including authentication, access control, fair-use scheduling policies, and GDPR-compliant data handling for multi-institutional use.
papers.abstract: This paper presents a feasibility study on the deployment of a European Deep Inference Fabric (eDIF), an NDIF-compatible infrastructure designed to support mechanistic interpretability research on large language models. The need for widespread accessibility of LLM interpretability infrastructure in Europe drives this initiative to democratize advanced model analysis capabilities for the research community. The project introduces a GPU-based cluster hosted at Ansbach University of Applied Sciences and interconnected with partner institutions, enabling remote model inspection via the NNsight API. A structured pilot study involving 16 researchers from across Europe evaluated the platform's technical performance, usability, and scientific utility. Users conducted interventions such as activation patching, causal tracing, and representation analysis on models including GPT-2 and DeepSeek-R1-70B. The study revealed a gradual increase in user engagement, stable platform performance throughout, and a positive reception of the remote experimentation capabilities. It also marked the starting point for building a user community around the platform. Identified limitations such as prolonged download durations for activation data as well as intermittent execution interruptions are addressed in the roadmap for future development. This initiative marks a significant step towards widespread accessibility of LLM interpretability infrastructure in Europe and lays the groundwork for broader deployment, expanded tooling, and sustained community collaboration in mechanistic interpretability research.

papers.title: Beyond Interpretability: The Gains of Feature Monosemanticity on Model Robustness
papers.research_question: Does feature monosemanticity, which improves interpretability, also improve model robustness, challenging the accuracy-interpretability tradeoff?
papers.core_contribution: This paper challenges the accuracy-interpretability tradeoff by showing that monosemantic features not only enhance interpretability but also provide concrete gains in model robustness across various scenarios including noise, few-shot learning, and out-of-domain generalization.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that monosemanticity offers advantages beyond interpretability, improving model robustness across multiple learning scenarios, and advocates for exploring its broader learning benefits.
papers.key_findings:
Monosemantic features (from NCL or SAE) are more robust than polysemantic features under linear probing with label noise and input noise.
Maintaining monosemanticity during finetuning (via non-negative tuning) reduces overfitting and improves performance in few-shot and noisy-label settings.
MonoLoRA, a sparse variant of LoRA, better preserves alignment safety while maintaining task performance when finetuning LLMs on small datasets.
Empirical analysis shows that classifiers with higher robustness under noise rely more on monosemantic features.
Theoretical analysis on a toy model indicates monosemantic features have better linear separability under noise, leading to more robust decision boundaries.
papers.abstract: Deep learning models often suffer from a lack of interpretability due to polysemanticity, where individual neurons are activated by multiple unrelated semantics, resulting in unclear attributions of model behavior. Recent advances in monosemanticity, where neurons correspond to consistent and distinct semantics, have significantly improved interpretability but are commonly believed to compromise accuracy. In this work, we challenge the prevailing belief of the accuracy-interpretability tradeoff, showing that monosemantic features not only enhance interpretability but also bring concrete gains in model performance. Across multiple robust learning scenarios-including input and label noise, few-shot learning, and out-of-domain generalization-our results show that models leveraging monosemantic features significantly outperform those relying on polysemantic features. Furthermore, we provide empirical and theoretical understandings on the robustness gains of feature monosemanticity. Our preliminary analysis suggests that monosemanticity, by promoting better separation of feature representations, leads to more robust decision boundaries. This diverse evidence highlights the generality of monosemanticity in improving model robustness. As a first step in this new direction, we embark on exploring the learning benefits of monosemanticity beyond interpretability, supporting the long-standing hypothesis of linking interpretability and robustness. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/PKU-ML/Beyond_Interpretability}.

papers.title: Explaining by Removing: A Unified Framework for Model Explanation
papers.research_question: How are existing model explanation methods related, and when is one method preferable to another?
papers.core_contribution: The paper presents a unified framework for removal-based explanations, characterizing 26 existing methods along three dimensions (feature removal, model behavior, summary technique) and establishing connections to cooperative game theory, information theory, and cognitive psychology.
papers.conclusion: The unified framework helps practitioners better understand model explanation tools and offers a strong theoretical foundation for future explainability research.
papers.key_findings:
The framework unifies 26 existing explanation methods, including SHAP, LIME, Meaningful Perturbations, and permutation tests.
The framework reveals that many methods are neighbors in the space of choices, differing in only one or two dimensions.
The conditional distribution removal strategy is the only approach consistent with probability axioms and gives all removal-based explanations an information-theoretic interpretation.
The Shapley value has advantages over other summary techniques due to its game-theoretic properties.
Feature removal is a simple application of subtractive counterfactual reasoning from cognitive psychology.
papers.limitation: The framework only covers removal-based explanation methods, and there are many methods that do not rely on the feature removal principle.
papers.abstract: Researchers have proposed a wide variety of model explanation approaches, but it remains unclear how most methods are related or when one method is preferable to another. We describe a new unified class of methods, removal-based explanations, that are based on the principle of simulating feature removal to quantify each feature's influence. These methods vary in several respects, so we develop a framework that characterizes each method along three dimensions: 1) how the method removes features, 2) what model behavior the method explains, and 3) how the method summarizes each feature's influence. Our framework unifies 26 existing methods, including several of the most widely used approaches: SHAP, LIME, Meaningful Perturbations, and permutation tests. This newly understood class of explanation methods has rich connections that we examine using tools that have been largely overlooked by the explainability literature. To anchor removal-based explanations in cognitive psychology, we show that feature removal is a simple application of subtractive counterfactual reasoning. Ideas from cooperative game theory shed light on the relationships and trade-offs among different methods, and we derive conditions under which all removal-based explanations have information-theoretic interpretations. Through this analysis, we develop a unified framework that helps practitioners better understand model explanation tools, and that offers a strong theoretical foundation upon which future explainability research can build.

papers.title: Causal AI for Data Scientists: A Framework to Automate Discovery of Causal Relationships in Noisy Datasets
papers.research_question: How can we develop a robust framework for causal discovery in noisy datasets with latent confounding?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a framework that integrates mechanistic interpretability with causal inference to discover causal relationships in noisy datasets, validated on synthetic and real-world data.
papers.conclusion: The framework demonstrates superior performance in identifying robust, interpretable causal structures in noisy, high-dimensional systems, offering a valuable tool for advancing causal inference in machine learning.
papers.key_findings:
The framework outperforms existing methods (NOTEARS, DAG-GNN) in accuracy and Structural Hamming Distance (SHD).
It identifies monosemantic and polysemantic variables through Causal Effect Strength (CES), Intervention Specificity (IS), and Polysemanticity Score (PS).
It achieves high modularity in latent representations, with the latent layer showing the strongest separation.
It successfully recovers known causal relationships in clinical (e.g., medication to blood pressure) and climate (e.g., pressure to temperature) data.
Mediation analysis reveals direct and indirect causal pathways, quantifying the role of latent mediators.
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> In the pursuit of advancing causal discovery methodologies, this research introduces a robust framework designed to navigate environments laden with noise and latent confounding. By integrating mechanistic interpretability with causal inference, the framework facilitates the structural disentanglement of complex causal influences, enabling a more transparent understanding of underlying mechanisms.The approach is validated using both synthetic datasets (Noisy-CausalSim, Sim-NCE+) and real-world datasets (MIMIC-IV clinical data and NOAA climate records), demonstrating versatility across diverse contexts. Key metrics—Causal Effect Strength (CES), Intervention Specificity (IS), and Polysemanticity Score (PS)—are employed to quantify the magnitude, focus, and dispersion of causal effects. Findings reveal that variables with high CES and low IS values act as monosemantic agents, exerting targeted influence, while higher PS scores indicate polysemantic variables affecting multiple targets.The framework's encoder-decoder architecture aligns latent representations with causal graphs, enhancing interpretability. Mediation analysis uncovers indirect causal pathways, highlighting the role of latent variables in effect transmission. Compared to traditional methods like NOTEARS and DAG-GNN, the proposed approach achieves superior performance, evidenced by higher CES and IS scores and lower Structural Hamming Distance (SHD).This work advances causal inference by providing tools for uncovering modular and interpretable causal structures, even amidst noise and latent confounding. The combination of mechanistic interpretability methods like activation patching and attention saliency allows for a more profound comprehension of the mechanisms of machine learning models. By closing the black-box prediction and causal processes underlying, this method not only increases the transparency but also the trustworthiness of causal AI systems. In addition, its applicability to a wide range of datasets demonstrates its flexibility and potential generalizability to a variety of fields.

papers.title: What can attribution methods show us about chemical language models?
papers.research_question: How can attribution methods be used to explain the predictions of a chemical language model for aqueous solubility?
papers.core_contribution: The adapted transformer-specific attribution method produces sparse attributions that reflect how the model maps molecular strings to its latent space, while SHAP provides sensible atom-level attributions but fails to explain functional groups relevant to solubility.
papers.conclusion: Attribution methods provide insight into how chemical language models represent molecules, but current techniques have limitations in explaining solubility predictions in terms of functional groups, instead revealing how the model organizes its latent space.
papers.key_findings:
Fine-tuning the MegaMolBART encoder significantly improves aqueous solubility prediction accuracy.
The transformer-specific attribution method (using the hRi token) yields sparse attributions that are characteristic of how the model represents molecular similarity in its latent space.
SHAP provides chemically sensible attributions (e.g., highlighting electronegative atoms) but does not explain predictions at the level of functional groups.
The fine-tuned model's latent space becomes linearly separable with respect to solubility along the first principal component.
The transformer-specific attribution method cannot propagate negative gradient information, limiting its ability to attribute negative contributions to solubility.
papers.limitation:
The transformer-specific attribution method cannot propagate negative gradient information, preventing attribution of features that negatively contribute to solubility.
SHAP does not capture functional group-level explanations for solubility predictions.
ECFP-based models are less predictive and their explanations are coarse-grained.
future_direction: Using the attributions to design focused, informative chemical datasets by creating training examples that contravene the model's predictions.
papers.abstract: Language models trained on molecular string representations have shown strong performance in predictive and generative tasks. However, practical applications require not only making accurate predictions, but also explainability - the ability to explain the reasons and rationale behind the predictions. In this work, we explore explainability for a chemical language model by adapting a transformer-specific and a model-agnostic input attribution technique. We fine-tune a pretrained model to predict aqueous solubility, compare training and architecture variants, and evaluate visualizations of attributed relevance. The model-agnostic SHAP technique provides sensible attributions, highlighting the positive influence of individual electronegative atoms, but does not explain the model in terms of functional groups or explain how the model represents molecular strings internally to make predictions. In contrast, the adapted transformer-specific explainability technique produces sparse attributions, which cannot be directly attributed to functional groups relevant to solubility. Instead, the attributions are more characteristic of how the model maps molecular strings to its latent space, which seems to represent features relevant to molecular similarity rather than functional groups. These findings provide insight into the representations underpinning chemical language models, which we propose may be leveraged for the design of informative chemical spaces for training more accurate, advanced and explainable models.

papers.title: Network Dissection: Quantifying Interpretability of Deep Visual Representations
papers.research_question: How can we quantify the interpretability of latent representations in CNNs by measuring the alignment between individual hidden units and semantic concepts, and what factors affect this interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces Network Dissection, a framework for quantifying the interpretability of CNN representations by evaluating the alignment between individual convolutional units and a broad set of semantic concepts, and uses it to show interpretability is an axis-aligned property affected by architecture, training data, and regularization.
papers.conclusion: Network Dissection provides a method to quantify interpretability in CNNs, revealing that interpretability is an axis-aligned property indicative of partially disentangled representations, and is influenced by network architecture, training data, and training techniques.
papers.key_findings:
Interpretability of units is not axis-independent; random rotations of the representation significantly reduce the number of unique concept detectors, indicating interpretability is a special alignment learned by the network.
Deeper network architectures (ResNet > VGG > GoogLeNet > AlexNet) and training on scene-centric data (Places) lead to more interpretable units (more unique concept detectors).
Self-supervised training tasks produce fewer object detectors and more texture detectors compared to supervised training, and the form of self-supervision (e.g., colorization) affects which concepts emerge.
Batch normalization significantly reduces interpretability, while dropout and different random initializations have less impact on the final level of interpretability.
Widening a convolutional layer (increasing the number of units) can increase the number of unique concept detectors without significantly harming classification accuracy.
papers.limitation: Network dissection works only as well as the underlying dataset; if a unit matches a human-understandable concept that is absent in Broden, it will not score well for interpretability.
future_direction: Expanding the Broden dataset to include more kinds of visual concepts.
Finding ways to capture the benefits of batch normalization without destroying interpretability.
papers.abstract: We propose a general framework called Network Dissection for quantifying the interpretability of latent representations of CNNs by evaluating the alignment between individual hidden units and a set of semantic concepts. Given any CNN model, the proposed method draws on a data set of concepts to score the semantics of hidden units at each intermediate convolutional layer. The units with semantics are labeled across a broad range of visual concepts including objects, parts, scenes, textures, materials, and colors. We use the proposed method to test the hypothesis that interpretability is an axis-independent property of the representation space, then we apply the method to compare the latent representations of various networks when trained to solve different classification problems. We further analyze the effect of training iterations, compare networks trained with different initializations, and measure the effect of dropout and batch normalization on the interpretability of deep visual representations. We demonstrate that the proposed method can shed light on characteristics of CNN models and training methods that go beyond measurements of their discriminative power.

papers.title: A Unified Theory of Sparse Dictionary Learning in Mechanistic Interpretability: Piecewise Biconvexity and Spurious Minima
papers.research_question: Why do sparse dictionary learning (SDL) methods consistently produce polysemantic features, feature absorption, and dead neurons, and what is the theoretical understanding of these phenomena?
papers.core_contribution: Develops a unified theoretical framework for sparse dictionary learning (SDL) that explains failure modes like feature absorption and dead neurons via piecewise biconvex optimization and non-identifiability, and proposes feature anchoring to improve feature recovery.
papers.conclusion: The theoretical framework explains persistent failure modes in SDL methods, and feature anchoring provides an effective, method-agnostic technique to improve feature recovery by reducing underdetermination.
papers.key_findings:
SDL optimization exhibits piecewise biconvex structure, enabling analysis of its landscape.
SDL suffers from non-identifiability, leading to spurious minima that result in polysemantic features.
Feature absorption arises naturally from hierarchical concept structures and corresponds to partial minima.
Feature anchoring, which constrains a subset of features to known directions, significantly improves feature recovery across SDL methods.
Dead neuron resampling helps escape spurious local minima in large language models.
papers.limitation:
Theoretical analysis relies on the Linear Representation Hypothesis, which assumes features are linear directions; this may not hold for all representations.
The synthetic benchmark, while controlled, may not capture all complexities of real-world data.
Feature anchoring requires anchor features, which may be difficult to obtain in some settings.
future_direction: Extending the theory to non-linear representations.
Applying feature anchoring to more domains and real-world tasks.
Integrating anchoring with other SDL improvements and scaling to larger models.
papers.abstract: As AI models achieve remarkable capabilities across diverse domains, understanding what representations they learn and how they encode concepts has become increasingly important for both scientific progress and trustworthy deployment. Recent works in mechanistic interpretability have widely reported that neural networks represent meaningful concepts as linear directions in their representation spaces and often encode diverse concepts in superposition. Various sparse dictionary learning (SDL) methods, including sparse autoencoders, transcoders, and crosscoders, are utilized to address this by training auxiliary models with sparsity constraints to disentangle these superposed concepts into monosemantic features. These methods are the backbone of modern mechanistic interpretability, yet in practice they consistently produce polysemantic features, feature absorption, and dead neurons, with very limited theoretical understanding of why these phenomena occur. Existing theoretical work is limited to tied-weight sparse autoencoders, leaving the broader family of SDL methods without formal grounding. We develop the first unified theoretical framework that casts all major SDL variants as a single piecewise biconvex optimization problem, and characterize its global solution set, non-identifiability, and spurious optima. This analysis yields principled explanations for feature absorption and dead neurons. To expose these pathologies under full ground-truth access, we introduce the Linear Representation Bench. Guided by our theory, we propose feature anchoring, a novel technique that restores SDL identifiability, substantially improving feature recovery across synthetic benchmarks and real neural representations.

papers.title: Emergence of Biological Structural Discovery in General-Purpose Language Models
papers.research_question: Can general-purpose language models infer biological structural logic through abstract reasoning without domain-specific training, or is it dependent on massive biological data?
papers.core_contribution: General-purpose language models possess an emergent capability for biological structural discovery through cross-modal transfer from linguistic syntax, enabling zero-shot performance on tasks like protein homology detection without domain-specific training.
papers.conclusion: The deep isomorphism between human language and biological sequences suggests that syntax is a universal property of organized information, and general-purpose LLMs can serve as powerful probes for decoding biological structure without domain-specific training.
papers.key_findings:
A GPT-2 model fine-tuned on English paraphrasing achieves ~84% zero-shot accuracy in protein homology detection, demonstrating cross-modal syntactic transfer.
Scaling to large models like Qwen-3 reveals a phase transition to near-perfect accuracy on standard tasks and maintains 75% precision on remote homology datasets.
Chain-of-Thought analysis shows that models perform 'mental folding', leveraging implicit structural knowledge for reasoning beyond sequence alignment.
The capability extends to DNA homology and Central Dogma mapping, with performance varying based on model scale and pre-training exposure.
The BioPAWS benchmark is introduced to standardize evaluation of cross-modal biological understanding in LLMs.
papers.limitation: Generative tasks such as de novo design of functional enzymes may lead to biologically plausible but physically unstable structures due to hallucinations.
future_direction: Hybrid architecture using general LLMs as high-level architects and domain-specific models as engineers to enforce physical constraints.
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> Large language models (LLMs) are evolving into engines for scientific discovery, yet the assumption that biological understanding requires domain-specific pre-training remains unchallenged. Here, we report that general-purpose LLMs possess an emergent capability for biological structural discovery. First, we demonstrate that a small-scale GPT-2, fine-tuned solely on English paraphrasing, achieves ~84% zero-shot accuracy in protein homology detection, where network-based interpretability confirms a deep structural isomorphism between human language and the language of life. Scaling to massive models (e.g., Qwen-3) reveals a phase transition, achieving near-perfect accuracy (~100%) on standard tasks while maintaining 75% precision on specially constructed remote homology datasets. Chain-of-Thought interpretability reveals that these models transcend simple sequence alignment, leveraging implicit structural knowledge to perform reasoning akin to "mental folding." We formalize this cross-modal universality through the BioPAWS benchmark. Our work establishes a minimalist paradigm for AI for Science, proving that abstract logical structures distilled from human language constitute a powerful cognitive prior for decoding the complex syntax of biology.

papers.title: Weight Spectra Induced Efficient Model Adaptation
papers.research_question: How does fine-tuning modify the structural properties of weight matrices, and how can these insights be leveraged for more efficient fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces SpecLoRA, a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that leverages spectral analysis of weight matrices to selectively modulate the top singular directions, achieving improved performance over existing methods.
papers.conclusion: SpecLoRA provides an effective and efficient fine-tuning method by leveraging spectral insights, achieving state-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmarks.
papers.key_findings:
Fine-tuning primarily amplifies the top singular values of weight matrices while leaving the rest of the spectrum unchanged.
The top singular vectors of fine-tuned weights become nearly orthogonal to those of the pre-trained weights, indicating reorientation in task-specific directions.
SpecLoRA, which incorporates learnable rescaling of top singular directions, consistently outperforms existing PEFT methods across multiple benchmarks.
papers.limitation: SpecLoRA uses a fixed k for all layers and weight matrices, which may not be optimal across diverse network depths or parameter types.
papers.abstract: Large-scale foundation models have demonstrated remarkable versatility across a wide range of downstream tasks. However, fully fine-tuning these models incurs prohibitive computational costs, motivating the development of Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) methods such as LoRA, which introduces low-rank updates to pre-trained weights. Despite their empirical success, the underlying mechanisms by which PEFT modifies model parameters remain underexplored. In this work, we present a systematic investigation into the structural changes of weight matrices during fully fine-tuning. Through singular value decomposition (SVD), we reveal that fine-tuning predominantly amplifies the top singular values while leaving the remainder largely intact, suggesting that task-specific knowledge is injected into a low-dimensional subspace. Furthermore, we find that the dominant singular vectors are reoriented in task-specific directions, whereas the non-dominant subspace remains stable. Building on these insights, we propose a novel method that leverages learnable rescaling of top singular directions, enabling precise modulation of the most influential components without disrupting the global structure. Our approach achieves consistent improvements over strong baselines across multiple tasks, highlighting the efficacy of structurally informed fine-tuning.

papers.title: Causality is Key for Interpretability Claims to Generalise
papers.research_question: How can interpretability claims be made more rigorous and generalizable? The paper argues that causal inference specifies what constitutes a valid mapping from model activations to invariant high-level structures and the evidence needed to support such claims.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a causal framework for interpretability, arguing that claims should be stated in the language of causal inference and identifiability to ensure they generalize. It uses Pearl's causal hierarchy to diagnose claim-evidence mismatches and causal representation learning to specify assumptions.
papers.conclusion: Interpretability claims should be grounded in causal inference to ensure they generalize, and practitioners should use a causal framework to align methods, evidence, and claims.
papers.key_findings:
There is a frequent gap between the evidence provided by interpretability methods (e.g., associational) and the strength of the claims made (e.g., interventional or counterfactual).
A pilot study of 50 papers found roughly half of interpretability claims can admit a stronger interpretation than the evidence supports, indicating a field-wide terminological challenge.
papers.abstract: Interpretability research on large language models (LLMs) has yielded important insights into model behaviour, yet recurring pitfalls persist: findings that do not generalise, and causal interpretations that outrun the evidence. Our position is that causal inference specifies what constitutes a valid mapping from model activations to invariant high-level structures, the data or assumptions needed to achieve it, and the inferences it can support. Specifically, Pearl's causal hierarchy clarifies what an interpretability study can justify. Observations establish associations between model behaviour and internal components. Interventions (e.g., ablations or activation patching) support claims how these edits affect a behavioural metric (\eg, average change in token probabilities) over a set of prompts. However, counterfactual claims -- i.e., asking what the model output would have been for the same prompt under an unobserved intervention -- remain largely unverifiable without controlled supervision. We show how causal representation learning (CRL) operationalises this hierarchy, specifying which variables are recoverable from activations and under what assumptions. Together, these motivate a diagnostic framework that helps practitioners select methods and evaluations matching claims to evidence such that findings generalise.

papers.title: Rethinking the Role of Scale for In-Context Learning: An Interpretability-based Case Study at 66 Billion Scale
papers.research_question: Are all LLM components really needed to perform in-context learning?
papers.core_contribution: Only a core nucleus of attention heads and feed forward networks (FFNs) in a large language model (OPT-66B) are important for in-context learning across a wide variety of tasks, and these important heads overlap with task-agnostic induction heads.
papers.conclusion: Large language models may be undertrained for in-context learning, and the findings motivate investigating pre-training regimes to increase the number of important model components for in-context learning.
papers.key_findings:
~70% of attention heads and ~20% of FFNs can be removed with minimal decline in in-context learning task performance.
Important attention heads are primarily clustered in the intermediate layers of the model.
There is substantial overlap in the set of attention heads (un)important for in-context learning across tasks and number of in-context examples (shots).
A small set of attention heads in OPT-66B score highly on primitive induction operations (prefix matching and copying).
These induction heads overlap with task-specific important heads, indicating they are capable of more sophisticated in-context learning behaviors.
papers.limitation:
No causal link is claimed between induction heads and sophisticated in-context learning capabilities; deeper investigation is needed.
The study uses only up to 5 in-context examples and random selection of examples.
All downstream tasks are monolingual.
future_direction: Increase the number and strength of induction heads via auxiliary pre-training objectives for primitives like prefix matching and copying.
Investigate and improve (pre-)training regimes to increase the number of important model components for in-context learning.
Replicate the study with instruction-tuned model variants (e.g., OPT-IML).
papers.abstract: Hritik Bansal, Karthik Gopalakrishnan, Saket Dingliwal, Sravan Bodapati, Katrin Kirchhoff, Dan Roth. Proceedings of the 61st Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2023.

papers.title: CoT Vectors: Transferring and Probing the Reasoning Mechanisms of LLMs
papers.research_question: Can we transfer the essence of Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning into LLMs in a compact, reusable, and efficient way? Also, how can CoT Vectors be used to probe the underlying mechanisms of reasoning in LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CoT Vectors, compact representations that encode task-general, multi-step reasoning knowledge, and proposes Learnable CoT Vectors optimized via a teacher-student framework for more stable and robust guidance.
papers.conclusion: CoT Vectors extend the task vector paradigm to multi-step reasoning, and Learnable CoT Vectors provide stronger and more stable gains, while also serving as a valuable probe into the mechanisms and organization of reasoning in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Extracted CoT Vectors show a U-shaped performance curve across layers, revealing a three-stage reasoning process (perception, reasoning, expression) in LLMs.
Learnable CoT Vectors outperform extracted vectors and are more stable across layers.
CoT Vectors achieve performance comparable to parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods like LoRA while requiring orders of magnitude fewer trainable parameters.
The effectiveness of CoT Vectors varies with latent space structure, information density, acquisition mechanisms, and pre-training differences.
CoT Vectors can be used as a probe to analyze the functional organization of reasoning in LLMs.
papers.limitation:
Performance variability in intermediate layers highlights structural limitations, suggesting that task-level vectors may not fully capture intra-task diversity.
CoT Vectors can sometimes interfere with correct reasoning paths and lead to incorrect answers, as shown in case studies.
future_direction: Explore finer-grained or adaptive vectorization strategies to improve robustness and generalization.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting has emerged as a powerful approach to enhancing the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs). However, existing implementations, such as in-context learning and fine-tuning, remain costly and inefficient. To improve CoT reasoning at a lower cost, and inspired by the task vector paradigm, we introduce CoT Vectors, compact representations that encode task-general, multi-step reasoning knowledge. Through experiments with Extracted CoT Vectors, we observe pronounced layer-wise instability, manifesting as a U-shaped performance curve that reflects a systematic three-stage reasoning process in LLMs. To address this limitation, we propose Learnable CoT Vectors, optimized under a teacher-student framework to provide more stable and robust guidance. Extensive evaluations across diverse benchmarks and models demonstrate that CoT Vectors not only outperform existing baselines but also achieve performance comparable to parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods, while requiring fewer trainable parameters. Moreover, by treating CoT Vectors as a probe, we uncover how their effectiveness varies due to latent space structure, information density, acquisition mechanisms, and pre-training differences, offering new insights into the functional organization of multi-step reasoning in LLMs. The source code will be released.

papers.title: Interpreting Language Models Through Concept Descriptions: A Survey
papers.research_question: The paper surveys the field of concept descriptions for model components, aiming to answer questions about common methods and data sources, best practices for evaluation, observed trends, and key gaps and future directions.
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides the first survey of the emerging field of concept descriptions for model components and abstractions, charting methods, evaluation techniques, and datasets, and identifies a growing demand for rigorous causal evaluation and provides a roadmap for future research.
papers.conclusion: The use of LLMs to generate concept descriptions is a notable step towards demystifying LLMs, with a trajectory from labeling neurons to abstractions and maturing evaluation methods, but the path to verifiable causal mechanisms is not yet fully paved and costs and faithfulness concerns remain.
papers.key_findings:
Recognition of neuron polysemanticity has driven adoption of model abstractions like Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and frameworks for multiple concepts per feature.
Evaluation of concept descriptions is maturing, with multi-faceted metrics assessing predictive power, input accuracy, and causal faithfulness.
The field is moving from labeling individual neurons to higher-level abstractions like SAEs and circuits.
There is a need for more rigorous causal evaluation and standardized benchmarks.
papers.limitation:
Focus limited to natural language concept descriptions for internal model components and abstractions, excluding other interpretability work.
Substantial computational and financial costs associated with the methods surveyed.
Focus on English-language models and text corpora, with generalization to other languages being an open question.
future_direction: Scaling automated description methods to circuits.
Applying concept description methods to new data domains and modalities.
Analyzing the interpreters (LLMs) themselves to understand biases and limitations in generated descriptions.
papers.abstract: Understanding the decision-making processes of neural networks is a central goal of mechanistic interpretability. In the context of Large Language Models (LLMs), this involves uncovering the underlying mechanisms and identifying the roles of individual model components such as neurons and attention heads, as well as model abstractions such as the learned sparse features extracted by Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs). A rapidly growing line of work tackles this challenge by using powerful generator models to produce open-vocabulary, natural language concept descriptions for these components. In this paper, we provide the first survey of the emerging field of concept descriptions for model components and abstractions. We chart the key methods for generating these descriptions, the evolving landscape of automated and human metrics for evaluating them, and the datasets that underpin this research. Our synthesis reveals a growing demand for more rigorous, causal evaluation. By outlining the state of the art and identifying key challenges, this survey provides a roadmap for future research toward making models more transparent.

papers.title: From Human Explanation to Model Interpretability: A Framework Based on Weight of Evidence
papers.research_question: How can we design interpretability methods that are meaningful to humans, inspired by the study of human explanation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a human-centered framework for interpretability based on weight of evidence, generating explanations that are contrastive, modular, and parsimonious.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a framework for interpretability based on weight of evidence, showing it can generate human-centered explanations that are usable and robust.
papers.key_findings:
The weight of evidence (WoE) can be adapted to high-dimensional, multi-class settings to generate human-centered explanations.
WoE explanations can be accurately estimated from finite samples and are robust to small input perturbations.
A user study with ML practitioners showed that WoE explanations are usable, though some struggled with concepts like prior class probabilities.
The framework adheres to design principles derived from human explanation literature: contrastive, exhaustive, modular, understandable, and parsimonious.
The method is compared to LIME and SHAP, showing competitive robustness on benchmark datasets.
papers.limitation:
The WoE requires access to conditional likelihoods, which may be difficult to estimate for complex data types like images.
The user study had a limited number of participants and focused on ML practitioners, which may not generalize to other user groups.
future_direction: Adapting modern density estimation methods for complex data types like images to widen applicability.
Conducting follow-up user studies to investigate design choices like class partitioning techniques.
Longitudinal field studies with participants using their own models and data.
papers.abstract: We take inspiration from the study of human explanation to inform the design and evaluation of interpretability methods in machine learning. First, we survey the literature on human explanation in philosophy, cognitive science, and the social sciences, and propose a list of design principles for machine-generated explanations that are meaningful to humans. Using the concept of weight of evidence from information theory, we develop a method for generating explanations that adhere to these principles. We show that this method can be adapted to handle high-dimensional, multi-class settings, yielding a flexible framework for generating explanations. We demonstrate that these explanations can be estimated accurately from finite samples and are robust to small perturbations of the inputs. We also evaluate our method through a qualitative user study with machine learning practitioners, where we observe that the resulting explanations are usable despite some participants struggling with background concepts like prior class probabilities. Finally, we conclude by surfacing design implications for interpretability tools in general.

papers.title: Rethinking LLM-as-a-Judge: Representation-as-a-Judge with Small Language Models via Semantic Capacity Asymmetry
papers.research_question: Can small language models serve as efficient evaluators by leveraging internal representations, even when their generation is poor?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes the Semantic Capacity Asymmetry Hypothesis and introduces INSPECTOR, a probing-based framework that extracts evaluation signals from small model representations, enabling efficient and accurate reference-free evaluation.
papers.conclusion: Small LMs retain strong evaluative signals in their internal representations, and the Representation-as-a-Judge paradigm via INSPECTOR offers a scalable and interpretable solution for evaluation and data curation.
papers.key_findings:
Small LMs encode rich evaluative signals in their hidden states despite weak generation.
Probing internal representations with INSPECTOR outperforms prompt-based evaluation with small LMs and closely approximates large LLM judges.
The Semantic Capacity Asymmetry Hypothesis is supported: evaluation requires less semantic capacity than generation.
Probing classifiers can serve as reliable data filters for supervised fine-tuning, leading to performance gains.
Larger LLMs do not necessarily provide stronger evaluation signals than smaller ones.
papers.limitation:
Multiclass prediction performance of probing classifiers is modest (50-60%) compared to binary classification.
Out-of-distribution generalization for multiclass probing is limited, with F1 scores dropping significantly.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are widely used as reference-free evaluators via prompting, but this "LLM-as-a-Judge" paradigm is costly, opaque, and sensitive to prompt design. In this work, we investigate whether smaller models can serve as efficient evaluators by leveraging internal representations instead of surface generation. We uncover a consistent empirical pattern: small LMs, despite with weak generative ability, encode rich evaluative signals in their hidden states.
